utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case name IT-95-14/2-T, the Prosecutor versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lopez-Terres.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Excuse me. Witness C, yesterday you mentioned the various attacks that took place during the week of 19 to 26 October, 1992. Could you tell us this morning why, in your opinion, the HVO in Novi Travnik launched the attacks at that point?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Objection. This calls for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: This calls for pure opinion as to why members of the opposition did something, without a basis, without knowledge of this witness as an expert or someone who has reason to know why the other side was doing what it was doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He can say what he knows. He can say if, as far as he could see, there was any reason for this attack. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Excuse me, please, Mr. Lopez-Terres. In respect of the objections, I believe that the Presiding Judge had already indicated the issues that could be raised in respect of objections. This is an International Tribunal, and we are all working in a particular spirit that is a way of trying to avoid small procedural complications that are of no point. I believe that we have to respect the criteria set by the President, that is, to try to have the proceedings operate properly when it's being understood that the Judges will form their own opinions at the proper time in respect of what is being done. Unless there is an absolutely fundamental objection affecting the entire proceedings, I think we have to, in the future, refrain from making these pointless objections. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation)

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Witness C, could you tell us, in your opinion, what those reasons were, that is, the reasons why the HVO decided, during that week of 19 to 26 October, 1992, to launch the fighting in the city and in the region?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Since you asked for my opinion, I would, nevertheless --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It is no criticism of you. What I ruled was that opinion evidence is not admissible. What is admissible is if he knows of his own knowledge any reason why the attack should have been launched. He may know and he may not. So, Witness C, could you think about that question and tell us, of your own knowledge, if you know why an attack should have been launched.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: At the municipal headquarters of the armoured forces, I thought that the reason for the attack was the advancement in part of the town of Novi Travnik so as to reach the Bratstvo plant and, thus, put out of control the whole territory of the town and, thus, presumably gain some strategic positions for further HVO plans. This is what the municipal headquarters thought was the principle reason for the attack in October 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Did the HVO carry out similar attacks, similar to what we're talking about, in other cities in Central Bosnia in that same period of October 1992, around that same date?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: The municipal headquarters of the defence also had information that during those days or, rather, on the 18th and 19th October, 1992, there were conflicts between the units of the BH army and the HVO units in Gornji Vakuf and Vitez. This was the information we had then.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Could you show us, Witness C, on the map that was already given to you at the beginning of your testimony, it is 26123, indicate the positions that you're speaking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) 26123. This one. The map of the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Could you show us the locations that you're referring to on that map, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: I mentioned two adjacent municipalities, Novi Travnik and Vitez or, rather, the town of Vitez, which is about 15 kilometres away from Novi Travnik, and the municipality of Gornji Vakuf or, rather, the town of Gornji Vakuf which here across Pavlovica, by short cut, is 37 kilometres away from Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: In addition to Gornji Vakuf and Vitez, were other municipalities attacked by the HVO during that same period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: During that period there was also an attack on the municipality of Prozor, as far as I know. I am not aware about what was going on in other municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Could you show us the city of Prozor on the map, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't think you can see it here. There is Makljen crossing here towards Jablanica is -- oh, no. Here it is. Here it is, the town of Prozor. Some 25 kilometres from Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness C.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Usher, you could take your seat again. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: We're still now after the fighting of October 1992. As far as you know, did the Novi Travnik HVO forces organise themselves or reorganise themselves, structure themselves, after the October conflict and especially was there a new brigade created in Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Right after the conflict in October, indeed, we know that a brigade was formed. It was the HVO brigade called Stjepan Tomasevic in Novi Travnik. I think there was a festival, a celebration, related to the establishment of that brigade which took place in November '92. As far as I know, the first Commander of that brigade was Mr. Malbasic from Vares.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: This Mr. Malbasic that you're speaking about, had he been operating in that position as Commander of that brigade for a long time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: The Commander of the Stjepan Tomasevic HVO Brigade in Novi Travnik, Mr. Boro Malbasic, was there until February or March. I would not know exactly when he was succeeded by Mr. Zeljko Sabljic who became the Commander of the Stjepan Tomasevic after him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Could you give us the name of the person who replaced him? I didn't really catch the name, the name that you gave us, the Commander who replaced mister --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. Boro Malbasic was succeeded by Mr. Zeljko Sabljic, born in Novi Travnik, who was an employee of Bratstvo. We knew each other for many years because we both worked for Bratstvo.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Do you have any information that would explain the reasons why Mr. Boro Malbasic was replaced after a few months of having been appointed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: I do not really have any precise information as to his short office there, but on the basis of meetings held in December and January, contacts between the Commander of the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade and the Commander of the brigade of the BH army which was set up in November in Novi Travnik, we know that he personally complained to the Commander that he could not keep the situation under control and that his command of the brigade was deemed moderate and that he had difficulty in keeping the brigade under control.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Therefore, he was allegedly replaced because he was too moderate? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I wonder, Mr. Lopez-Terres, if that is really going to help us. This is an opinion from the other side being given about a matter which we're going to have to decide, and I don't think it's very helpful evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: After that Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade had been created in Novi Travnik, did the BH army, of which you were a member, did it restructure itself as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. In the wake of it and the orders of the 3rd Corps, the formation of brigades began throughout the Central Bosnian territory which was under the area of responsibility of the 3rd Corps. Novi Travnik was one of the last municipalities which formed a brigade of the BH army because of certain dilemmas whether one should have one or two brigades in this area between the municipalities of Novi Travnik and Vitez. The 308th brigade of the BH army Novi Travnik was established on the orders of the Commander, Mr. Hadzihasanovic on the 18th of December, 1992. Four days later, the Commander of the brigade arrived, the man who was assigned to this duty, and he arrived from the territory of Sarajevo. It was mister --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter is sorry but we did not get the last name.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation)

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: This Mr. Zurapi, the Commander, shortly after being appointed was he arrested by the HVO forces?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Could you explain to us, please, under what circumstances that occurred?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: On the 13th January, 1993, there were talks between the Commander of the HVO Brigade and the Commander of the 308th Brigade of the BH army. I did not attend those talks personally. Then it was agreed that the Commander, Bislam Zurapi, should go around 9.00 to the building called Oskar to sign the conclusions that had been agreed upon that day. I know that because I was at the meeting when Mr. Zurapi was to go to that meeting, and we thought that it was not particularly wise and safe for him to attend that meeting, but because of the conclusion and duties he has assumed, he did go around 19.00 there, and then he did not call back for a long time. So that around 9.00 in the evening, people who were on duty in the brigade learned that Mr. Bislam Zurapi had been arrested and that he was somewhere in Busovaca. So we waited that night. Of course, we had contacts with the 3rd Corps. We were waiting for the return of the Commander because there was some suggestions that he would be released. Around 3.40, Mr. Zurapi came to the headquarters of the brigade and told us that he had been detained by the HVO members, taken to Busovaca, and kept there until after 2.00. After that he had been released, and he came back to the headquarters of the brigade around half past three.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: We're going to move to another subject now. Still referring to that same period that followed the attack of October, 1992, could you tell us whether, in the sector under the HVO force control, whether business people or inhabitants of Bosnian origin were the victims of criminal acts committed by HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: I mentioned already the effects of the second conflict in Novi Travnik, that is, in October, 1992, and that was a time when the majority of business outlets which were owned by Muslims, and I mentioned already the Videotech, restaurants, other shops and so on and so forth, when the majority of them were destroyed or demolished.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Were any people of Bosnian origin murdered?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: I already mentioned a murder from this October period. This was the murder of Mr. Dzemo Krnjic, owner of the Duga Pizzeria at the entrance into Novi Travnik next to the locality Bare. He was killed when he tried to put out a fire put to his premises, and we know that his body lay there for two days after the murder across the road from his business premises.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Did inhabitants of Bosnian origin -- were the people of Bosnian origin who were expelled from that sector at that point?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: In the course of the October conflict, there were very many breakings and enterings into Muslim flats presumably to search for weapons, but there were also instances of physical harassment and ill treatment of people by numerous HVO members, particularly in the area of Bare, which is a large borough, a large quarter in Novi Travnik, residential. That is where citizens were particularly ill treated. It somewhat declined in November, December, 1992, but then this ill treatment became again very intensive in January '93, and it did not stop until the 8th of June, 1993. It would sometimes decline as the number of the population decreased in this part of the town which was controlled by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Witness C, do you know whether the expulsions were the work exclusively of Novi Travnik HVO forces?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: The statements of all the inhabitants who, after the October meeting or during the October meeting, moved over to the part of the town which was behind the lines of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina told us, and I talked to very many families because very often there were families of members of the BH army and I had to see that they are accommodated. All of them said that there was ill treatment, harassment, or eviction, expulsion from flats by HVO members.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Let's move away from the period of October. You've already spoken about the period January to June, 1993. During the beginning of 1993, could one note in Novi Travnik that there were soldiers who had come from other regions, other regions of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. We received information from our units who were on the line, the Pavlovica-Opara to the town, and we also learned from the -- and according to the information of the 3rd Corps in the area of Novi Travnik and Vitez, three HVO buses had arrived from Herzegovina. We called them Herzegovinians. This happened on the 8th of January, 1993. Likewise, according to information of security bodies of the BH army, we subsequently also learned the name of that unit. It was the Bruno Busic Unit. That unit was -- I do not know how many soldiers stayed in Novi Travnik and how many were occupying some other positions, but they were in Novi Travnik as of the evening of January the 8th. As for the consequences which ensued, we know that those were soldiers from Herzegovina because all of the people that I talked to, after they had encountered the soldiers, told us that they were soldiers whom they could recognise by their speech, that they were HVO members who did not come from the territory of our municipality because, to begin with, people knew one another. And besides, they also have characteristic speech, a characteristic dialogue which was different.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Did your headquarters realise -- find any particular reason why it was necessary to go to Novi Travnik, into the neighbouring municipalities, speaking about that, as to have soldiers coming in from other regions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: At the brigade command, we could not really establish why -- how did these HVO units come from Herzegovina to Novi Travnik and perhaps some other places, but we thought that they were there to provoke some incidents so as to find pretext for renewed conflicts in Novi Travnik, because we knew that as of the 11th of January, '93, there were armed conflicts between HVO units and units -- and the Croatian army in Gornji Vakuf on one side and the units of the BH army on the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You just spoke about three buses of soldiers coming from Herzegovina. Could you tell us about how many soldiers were sent into the region?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. We thought that about 150 soldiers had arrived, three buses, and that was the information that we received, three buses. That is 150 HVO members, Bruno Busic Unit from Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: During the year 1993 but a little bit later, was the city of Novi Travnik blockaded by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Physical blockade impeding the movement of people and traffic after the end of the second conflict, apart from various incidents at the checkpoints, was none, so between the 1st of November, 1992, until the 13th April, 1993. After April 13th, 1993, after an incident which happened with soldiers belonging to the HVO, the soldiers allegedly disappeared or were arrested in an area controlled by the units of the BH army, so that as of 17.00 on that April 13, a blockade was established around the area so that we, who were in the territory of the municipality of Novi Travnik, could not go out to any other municipality for a couple of days. After that, some talks were conducted, and the commander of the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade and the commander of our brigade agreed that they would allow the passage of military -- of army units, including their shifts, food supply and ammunition, that is, for the units who were elsewhere on the front, that is, those who were confronted with this aggressor. We had a number of units who were in the area of Turbe so that after this 13th April, I think it was for a short while, only for seven or eight days, that we agreed about that passage. But blockade was still in force for the traffic of goods and other things. After that, we, from Novi Travnik, could not go anywhere, except for the movement of units, their shifts, and provision of food, ammunition and supplies for units on the front.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Lopez-Terres, you spoke about a blockade with the witness. Could you indicate clearly, because we don't really know what the meaning of this other blockade was? It was a very long answer, but, you, yourself, did not specify what you meant by "blockade." Did you mean that there was a total closure and that the witness should therefore answer briefly, because you've got to make the idea of the blockade clearer to the Trial Chamber so that we have a very specific idea of what it is that is at stake here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation)

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Witness C, the arrangements that were set into place after April, 1993, particularly, did they prevent access and leaving of the city of Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. From the town of Novi Travnik, for a longer period of time, we could not move in any direction. I'll show it on the map. We could not move towards Travnik because there was a blockade in that part of town towards Travnik or Vitez, so this is one single road. We could not move towards Gornji Vakuf either because there was a blockade in the region of Medenik where HVO units from Sebesici held ground. We could not move towards Bugojno either because via Rostovo there was a road that went to Bugojno. There was a blockade here three or four kilometres before Bugojno. There is yet another road via Mescema towards Travnik, and we could not move in that direction, either, because HVO units from the area of Travnik were in the region of Mescema and they had closed off that road as well. This total blockade went on for about seven to ten days, and then an agreement was reached that the blockade did not apply to the military units that were facing the Serb aggressor at the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You said, Witness C, that it was not possible for the Bosnian army forces in Novi Travnik to go to Vitez after 13 April?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's continue the testimony in respect of 1993. You have already mentioned the two first conflicts that took place in Novi Travnik, the first in June of 1992, and the second, in October of 1992. I would like you to speak to us now about the third conflict which was triggered in the city, and first could you tell us when, exactly, that conflict began, in a few words?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Combat action between the units of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the HVO units in the territory of the municipality of Novi Travnik began exactly on the 9th of June, 1993. Six days after the armed conflict had started in Travnik between the same units.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: How long did that third conflict last?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: The conflict that started on the 9th of June, 1993, lasted until the cease-fire was signed or, rather, the order that was signed by Mr. Rasim Delic and Mr. Ante Roso sometime around the 23rd or 24th of February, 1994, but I know it came into force, I mean, the cease-fire came into force on the 25th of February, 1994, so this conflict lasted from June, 1993, until February, 1994, incessantly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Usher, could you give the witness a document on which he can show us where the forces and the front line were in the city of Novi Travnik? I think that this document has already been submitted to the Tribunal, and it's Z1962(c).

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Witness C, is this document the one that you sent a copy to our office?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that's the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: So we can see on the document the confrontation line which was the one that you mentioned in your previous testimony about the October conflict, that this confrontation line, in fact, did not change very much at all since before that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: As the line of conflict on the 9th of June was practically along this line in town, just as it was on the 25th of October, 1992, when the second conflict was ending between the HVO units and the BH army units. The only difference is that the June line left the HVO at the workers' centre. They were not at the old high-rise, the one that I marked with number 1, as they were in October. In the October conflict, this high-rise, especially its top three floors, were the military stronghold of the HVO, and they used inflammable bullets and they set on fire high-rise three. So in June, the HVO units were only in the workers' council and the workers' building and, also, here, as they were in October 1992. They also remained at Streliste, and they had an HVO unit that was stationed there all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: On the document that you have in front of you, you can see a building, I think you've just referred to it. Is this the building known as Stari Soliter? Could you point it out to us? Stari Soliter, I think that that means in Serbo-Croat the "old high-rise," the "old building." Could you show it to us, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: The location of this building or, rather, this high-rise that we call the old high-rise, because it was the first multi-storey building in the town of Novi Travnik, it had ten storeys, and that is why everybody who lived there could tell it apart from all the other buildings that were built subsequently. Everybody called it the old high-rise and that's how everybody knew what building it was. So it is this high-rise that is about 20 to 25 metres away from the workers' centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: The building called Stari Soliter, was it the object of very, very serious attacks by the HVO and army attacks in June of 1993 and in the coming months that followed, rather.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: I would not say that it was heavy fighting but it really was of special interest to both sides or, rather, the soldiers that were in the workers' council and also for the members of the army who were using this building here, high-rise three, that burned down in the October conflict. Then from June onwards it was used as a military facility. The HVO probably had an interest in using this facility as -- for military purposes because it was as tall as the other buildings were. The members of the army who were in this part, in this high-rise here -- you can't see the line that I drew here, I did mark it though but with a different colour -- HVO soldiers tried to get into this high-rise but the members of the army did not allow this to happen because they kept it under fire. The entrance is on the west side. They did not let HVO soldiers get into this high-rise because it was only civilians who were in there and it was not a military stronghold of the units of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: What was the date that these confrontations began, that is, the confrontations in respect of the building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Practically immediately on the 9th of June. Immediately on the 9th of June this high-rise was a matter of controversy. The HVO units wanted to turn it into a military facility again as they did in the October conflict. So this building was in a zone between the two lines, you see. That is why the position of civilians who were in this building was extremely difficult. At the outset of the conflict on the 9th of June, in this high-rise there were 57 persons who were spending the night there in that high-rise.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: So this is while the building had -- while the fighting had begun there were still people in that building. You said there were 57 of them. Were they civilians? Were they military personnel?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: These were only civilians, except for two soldiers who had been army members before that, but they would go back home to spend the night. So they were spending the night with their families in this building. One of the soldiers was Zijad Muslic, and Suljo Silajdzic was the other one, because their families lived there. They came there on the 8th of June to spend the night that. The conflict broke out around 6.00 in the morning, so they happened to be there. All the rest were civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: There were women? There were children as well; is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Out of the 57 persons who were in the high-rise there were 18 children and 10 women. Those were the mothers of these children. Then there were another 10 women who did not have children and the rest were men.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You gave to officers, when you testified, the document on which you have the list of the inhabitants of that building, that is, document Z1963.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Usher, could you give that document to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Is this, in fact, the document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that's it. That is the list that I handed in to the investigator that I talked to, and I got the document from Safet Duvnjak who, at the time, was the President of the commission for exchanges appointed by the war presidency of Novi Travnik. So he had composed this list and I took it from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: On the list we see the names of the people who lived in the building. Were all of these inhabitants of Bosnian origin or were there Croats as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: In the building there were mostly Bosniaks but there were others too who were not Bosniaks, either families that lived in so-called mixed marriages or persons who were simply of a different ethnic background. For example, Josip Vujic and Ivanka Vujic, they're not Bosniaks. Also, Ivic Dusan. And there's Mira Kares, also not a Bosniak. There's also Natasa Krsin, who is also not a Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Lopez-Terres, so that the Judges can understand properly, we heard about mixed families and Bosniak families. Can I understand what that really is? When they talked about "mixed families," what is that exactly?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation)

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Could you explain that to us, Witness C. Explain what you mean by "mixed families." At least this is the way it was said in French, "mixed families."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: These are families where the husband or the wife were, for example, were a Bosniak, a Serb or a Croat, and the spouse belonged to a different ethnic group. We usually call these mixed marriages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Did the religious element influence the mixed character? I would like to know whether there was a religious element at stake here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation)

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: The distinction that you make, could we say that it was based on ethnic or only on religious factors?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, when we're talking about mixed marriages, we're only talking about the ethnic criterion. When we say that a marriage is a mixed marriage, then it is different from another marriage.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Witness C, in that building, that is -- that in the building, were the inhabitants armed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: As far as I know, in that building there weren't any soldiers who had weapons, although there were two persons who were members of the BH army before that. I already mentioned Zijad Muslic and Suljo Silajdzic, but they went home without any weapons. They left their weapons back at the unit, and they were supposed to go back and get their weapons again.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: About how long did the inhabitants of that building remain inside without being able to go out because they were caught by the fire?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: These 57, or from the 2nd of July onwards it was 56 inhabitants, they spent a three-month period between these two zones. That is to say, from the 9th of June until the 9th of September. All these three months they could not go out and no one could go in. No one could reach the inhabitants of this building.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: How did they get food? Was assistance brought to them from outside?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: They used the food supplies that these families happened to have, that is to say, the families who lived in the building itself. After the inhabitants of this building talked about this, after this period, in some apartments they had some food supplies or, rather, there were some empty apartments too where there were food supplies. So when they ran out of food, their own food, they went to these other apartments and got these extra food supplies. It was impossible to get any food to them. After two months had passed and when it was really critical for them in this apartment building, then at the beginning of August we managed to cover this distance between the Stari Soliter, the old high-rise, and this other place that I marked as number three, this is about 40 metres, a 40-metre distance, we managed to get a wire across. Then during a few evenings we managed to get some food supplies and some water supplies to the people in this building. We would use parcels of four or four and a half kilograms. We tried with bigger parcels too but then the wire broke down. So the wire was there for a couple of days but we couldn't send in more than four or four and a half kilograms via this wire.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Did the HVO soldiers prevent you from bringing in the provisions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, getting this assistance in and also bringing in messages and letters to this high-rise and, also, our soldiers who were in the old high-rise, this did not go on for a long period of time, eight to ten days at a maximum. This transport took place during the night when it was very dark and when others could not notice these parcels going across this wire. During the day, HVO soldiers, especially those at the position of the workers' centre, they were shooting at the wire every day and they tried to break it down. They did manage to do so after about ten days. So this was the third time that this wire was broken, and we never managed to connect the two again.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Did the BH army suggest to the HVO that the inhabitants of the building should be allowed out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: The first offer made by the army, especially by the war presidency of the municipality of Novi Travnik, was made to the HVO on the 2nd of July, 1993, when a physician from the army side went into a building and a physician from the HVO side, together with a representative of the International Red Cross. Then an offer was made to the HVO to carry out an evacuation of the inhabitants of this building and that it not be used as a military facility by either side. Even at those negotiations, the HVO asked that the inhabitants leave the building but that the building be handed over to them so that it remained under their control. The President of the commission who attended these negotiations could not accept that precondition and that is how the blockade of the high-rise continued.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: During those three months, did the HVO suggest that any exchange of individuals in the building be carried out, that is, an exchange for other people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: When the physicians came to see the inhabitants of the building on the 2nd -- the second time, that was on the 23rd of July, 1993, that was when the HVO asked for only an exchange of inhabitants to take place. That is to say, the inhabitants of this high-rise for inhabitants of Croat ethnic that were living in Senkovici and in another village. These are inhabitants who remained in this area and who did not dare go in anywhere. They remained after the conflict broke out on the 9th of June, 1993. I do not know exactly what number of inhabitants we are talking about, but I think that there were about 120 to 130 inhabitants, women, children, and elderly that were in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, the HVO proposal was to exchange the inhabitants of the building called Stari Soliter for Croatian people in the two villages in the sector under the BH army control, the two villages of Torine and Senkovici; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: How long had those villages been under the BH army control, that is, the two Croatian villages?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: The inhabitants of these two villages who were Croats lived together with the Bosniaks. For example, in Senkovici, they were a minority as compared to Bosniaks, whereas in Torine it was more or less the same number of Bosniaks and Croats. That is to say that this is a population that remained in their own houses after the third conflict had broken out between the HVO units and the army units, that is to say, on the 9th of June, 1993. These are people who lived there earlier on too. They remained there even after the conflict started because they were not directly affected in that village at first.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Could one deduce from everything you've said that there were other Croatian people living in other villages, Croatian villages under the HVO army control left their villages, as opposed to the ones in Senkovici and Torine?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: The inhabitants of other villages where there was a Croatian population and where there were HVO units, that is to say, that there was a front line in those villages, they left those villages in the night between the 15th and 16th of June, 1993. Before that, the line of contact between HVO and the BH army was in those villages. After that night, in the early morning hours, a strong explosion took place in the village of Hadzici and Pobrdani, and we did not know until the afternoon what kind of explosion this was. Only after 12.00 on that 16th of June, our units observed this, reconnoitred, and they saw that there weren't any inhabitants left in these villages. There wasn't any smoke coming out of the chimneys and you couldn't really see anything. Then the units started moving into this region where the HVO members and the Croats population was, and that is how we realise that in Hadzici and Pobrdani a larger quantity of weapons was destroyed. It was difficult to transport that along the road where the Croatian population was moving because we saw traces of this. Different things were dropped by them. They were moving towards Margetici, Hadzici, Zenepici, Pobrdani, and these other villages. That is to say, from Pobrdani via the village of Rude, and above Gornje Pecine, and then this went up to Mravinjac, Kamenjas where there was a line of contact between HVO soldiers and the Serb forces from the direction of the municipality of Donji Vakuf and Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: In respect of the Croatian population who left the villages, did they do that of their own free will or were they expelled by the BH army forces?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Those days this wasn't really any combat action and, therefore, there was no reason to evacuate that population. Perhaps I should mention to you that the army forces did not get into these villages throughout the day of the 16th of June, although, in fact, those villages were empty during that entire day. It is only from the 17th of June onwards that the members of the army went into those villages and realised that there were no people in there and no HVO units either. We do not know the reason why the population of these villages, together with the HVO, went and surrendered to the Serb side in the region of Kamenjas.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: As far as you know, at that period that we're speaking about, were there any orders given by the HVO to the Croatian population, orders to leave the area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: I am not aware of such an order, but I know that before that something similar happened to the Croat population in the municipality of Travnik. We had information that the members of HVO in Travnik, some part of them, and the Croat population of a part of the Travnik municipality, which gravitated towards Turbe and Vlasic, that they also left the territory of the municipality of Travnik and moved over to the Serb side in the area of Vlasic. That is HVO members and some parts of the Croat population.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You said that the inhabitants of the Stari Soliter building had remained locked in the building for three months. Could you speak to us about this exchange that occurred, because in the end there was an exchange, as you've said. Under what condition did the exchange take place and what was the date that it occurred?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: The old high-rise was entered by old HVO members on 9th September, '93 by moving from the ground floor of that building, and those were some business outlets. They brought a large quantity of explosives, put it on the wall which separated the offices from the entrance into flats, made a huge hole there and, thus, entered the residential part of that building and took out all the 56 inhabitants of this high-rise building and took them to the Sports Hall in HVO Travnik and there to the hotel called Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: How long did the people in the Stari Soliter building remain in that building before the exchange took place? How long were they kept there, rather?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Another seven days passed by until the exchange was agreed, that is, of those inhabitants and inhabitants of the villages of Senkovici and Turine. This was the express demand of the HVO as of the 23rd of July when this particular request was formulated. The war presidency of the Novi Travnik municipality and the commander of the BH army refused that kind of exchange of the population because that could indeed mean the expulsion of the Croat population by the army, and we've never accepted this condition. Lamentably, we agreed to that, under very hard conditions, only after those five to six -- that is on the principle of the exchange of population overall. We agreed only after this civilian population from the high-rise building was taken to the Sports Hall and were in the hands of the HVO and subjected to ill treatment. And since their lives were at risk, we agreed, even though reluctantly, to this exchange. And this exchange took place on the 17th of September, '93, somewhere between Novi Travnik and the locality of Trenica, some two kilometres away from the locality of Trenica in the municipality of Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Let's move to another point. During the fighting in June of '93, did the village called Lazine find itself taken by the HVO forces? I would like you to show us where the village is located on Exhibit Z2612/1. Could you put the document on the ELMO, please? Could you show us where the village of Lazine is on the map?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: The village of Lazine was under the neighbourhood community of Rankovici, and it is about a kilometre and a half or two from the seat of this neighbourhood community. It is below 929 reference point, which dominates over the area where the village is, and below Bucicka Ravan where the HVO kept a flow on it towards the village of Santici which was protected by the BH army units. The attack took place on the 29th of June, '93, sometime in the morning hours, about 9.00 or 10.00. Around 14.00, I was coming back with the commander from the road that is taking a roundabout from Novi Travnik, and in the village of Djakovici we saw that all the houses and stables were on fire in the village of Lazine in the evening, around 9.00. The commander of the unit, Suad Sakic reported to us -- he personally came to report to us at the headquarters that the village had been taken by HVO combatants, that all the houses had been burned down, and that there were very grave casualties among the BH army members and civilians who were defending the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Were the houses in the village of Lazine destroyed during the fighting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: They were not destroyed, they were simply burned down. A couple of days later, sometime in early July, I was in the village of Cakici, and one could see a house here and there or a stable standing, that is, not having been burned to the ground, but 90 per cent of all the buildings had burned down to the ground completely, both houses and stables. The same holds true of some seven or eight houses in a village, Gornji Rankovici, in a part of it, where there were also some seven or eight Muslim households, and their houses were set on fire that same day where the village of Lazine fell or, rather, where the front line near the village of Lazine of the Armijas line, I mean, and when they reached this village in the Novi Travnik municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: When, on the 29th of June, '93, the village of Lazine was taken, were there any BH army soldiers who were either killed or taken prisoner?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: The commander who informed us that evening at that meeting of the brigade command informed us that there were a number of casualties, including six civilians because they had taken some weapons either from soldiers who had been killed or had their own weapons. But at any rate, he informed us about the death of six civilians who were killed while defending the village. The commander of the brigade and the commander of the army recognised the status of combatants, so they said even though they were killed by civilians, subsequently they were recognised as the status of combatants in the army. Those houses were burned. On that particular day, we also learned that four soldiers had been captured and that one body, according to combatants, of those who took part in the fighting, one body remained lying on the ground in that village of Lazine. But the commander told us that there were four soldiers captured, including the leader of the squad, who was captured during that attack on the village of Lazine. Muhamed Sahinovic was his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You had information according to which the soldiers were captured. Could you tell us about that, please? That is, the four soldiers that you've just spoken about, were they released later on, were they exchanged?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: The 7th of July, '93, the exchange took place of bodies of killed soldiers. The bodies of the killed soldiers, Enver Omeragic, Ejub Omeragic, Hajdar Mujic and Muhamed Sahinovic's bodies we got in exchange on the 7th of July, and they were dead bodies. According to the post-mortem performed by the head of the medical corps, those two soldiers -- two of them were killed earlier and then buried, and there were marks on their bodies, indicating that they had been lying under the ground for about a week. According to Dr. Suad Grizic, Hajdar Mujic's body and Muhamed Sahinovic's body had been liquidated and massacred less than 24 hours before the exchange, that is, before the 7th of July, '93.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm finding it difficult to follow this evidence. How many bodies is it suggested were exchanged? Can you tell me that, Mr. Lopez-Terres?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) The witness is speaking about four soldiers who were exchanged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The bodies of four soldiers were exchanged. I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation)

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Do you have any information according to which the four soldiers that we're speaking about had been taken alive before the village was taken?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: According to the commander who led the units in the area of Lazine that day, Mr. Suad Sakic, and other soldiers who were there in the evening at the meeting of the brigade command, they said they knew for certain that those four soldiers had been captured alive, and that the body of Sulejman Omeragic, who had been killed, Sulejman Omeragic's body remained lying -- I mean he was killed and his body was lying in the village, whereas these four soldiers had been captured alive and taken away by HVO members.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Do you know where the four soldiers were being detained before the exchange of the bodies that you've just spoken about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: The first information as to the place of captivity of these men we received on the 13th of July, '93, after a captured Bosniak from the camp which was stationed at the compound of a construction enterprise in Stojkovici was exchanged. Mr. Fahrudin Hadzalic, who had been in this camp in Stojkovici when he was released, he told us that at this Stojkovici camp, four soldiers, members of the BH army, had also been detained in that camp. This was the first information as to the place of detention, which we learned from this detainee after he had been released and after we could take his statement at the brigade's command.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Could you show us the Stojkovici village, where the camp was, on the map?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: This camp was 2,5 or three kilometres away from the centre of Novi Travnik, the town, I mean, on the road to Travnik and Vitez. Here, in the area of the village of Stojkovici, is the seat of a construction company called Gradzevinar, which had a small building here next to the concrete manufacturing plant, and that is where the captured Bosniaks were kept as detainees. This is a side road some 100 metres away from the Novi Travnik-Travnik road, next to the village of Stojkovici, in front of the village of Stojkovici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Lopez-Terres, so that we can follow properly, could we have an idea about this village of Lazine and also Stojkovici that was just spoken about? When we say "village", what does that mean? Could we have some explanation by the witness of the number of people living there, what the population was?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation)

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Could you supplement the information, please, by informing us of what the Judge has just asked?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: The exact number, I could not tell you, but it was some 30 households, and when one thinks of the number of members of a household, perhaps 130 or 140 inhabitants of the village of Lazine. So it's a smallish village in the municipality of Novi Travnik, and as such, it was an integral part of the village of Rankovici, which is a larger locality, larger settlement, and it belonged to the neighbourhood community of Rankovici. This was one of the larger localities in the municipality of Novi Travnik, and I said that the villages of Rankovici and Stojkovici were villages, together with Butici, had the majority Croat population. The Muslim were the majority in Lazine and, to a certain degree, in the village of Gornji Rankovici with about seven or eight Muslim households.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: In this Stojkovici camp you have just spoken about, the people who were detained, were they civilian prisoners or were they military personnel?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: The first civilians were taken to the camp at Stojkovici on the 13th of July, '93. Those were civilians, Bosniaks, who had continued living in their houses around the Sports Hall in the town of Novi Travnik, across the river. Those were Semso Bradic, Sinan Prcanovic, Kasim Skrobo, Muhamed Kopcic's families and some refugees from Karaula who were staying with Mr. Hazim Skrobo. Others in this camp were Bosniaks who had not been expelled yet from the town and who had been living in the buildings next to the old hotel. Dr. Naida Muhamed, Dr. Fadil Tatarevic, Galib Merdan and some other civilians who were in that part; not very many of them. In the camp at Stojkovici, after -- from the 13th until the 25th of July, when the last prisoner was brought there, it was Naida Brkovic, a woman. There were altogether 21 persons, civilians, and that was the number of civilians who were detained in that camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, the four soldiers whose bodies were given back had also been detained in that camp after having been captured in Lazine?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. According to statements made by several inhabitants who had spent some time at the Stojkovici camp after the exchange, we learned that soldiers had also been kept there but on the ground floor of the same building. They were put up on a floor. That building had some staircase outside, and there were some premises in the loft, and on the ground floor there was another room, and allegedly, reportedly, they kept soldiers there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: The, approximately, 20 civilians who were there, how long did they remain in that camp, approximately?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, different prisoners stayed different periods of time there, but in the camp, those prisoners who spent there different periods of time were there between the 13th of June until the 30th of June, '93, when the civilians who were detained at the Stojkovici camp were exchanged. That is where we learned about the total number of civilians detained there and what happened, because we took statements from most of those who came out of the camp and came to the town, and then we took their statements from those who had been in the camp so that we knew what had happened to those 20-odd civilians during that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: According to information that you could get about those civilians, were you able to know whether some of them had been used by the HVO guards watching over them, used for forced labour?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: According to Muhamed Merdan's statement, and he was my worker and then was retired last April, he told me that those prisoners were ill-treated by some HVO members who simply happened to drop by, not by the guards, but by some other HVO soldiers who had just come to that facility and then ill treat civilians. As of the 2nd of July, '93, those detained soldiers -- I mean civilians, except Safet Imbrisimbegovic, who was an old man and who could not physically endure, according to the doctor, he was the only one, and in addition to those two women, these women Brkovic and another one called Sehida, all the others were taken to dig trenches and to serve in trenches in the area of the village of Zubici.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Is this village on the map?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, here it is. This is the village of Zubici, which is about here in the direction of Gornji Vakuf, perhaps a kilometre -- 1,5 to two kilometres away. This is where the separation line went between the HVO units and the BH army units. After the 2nd of July, those captured civilians were taken to the area of Zubici. They were driven in a truck by Hrvoje who came from the same company that I came to, and he would take them over from somewhere in the area of Rostovo by Vilim Coric, as they called him, a fiery one they called him on the Croat side, and he was the man who just brought him to the area of the village of Zubici and they were used to dig these trenches as of 8.00 in the morning and they worked until 16.00 to 17.00. It varied from one day to the other, and throughout that period of time until the exchange. During that period of time as they were digging those trenches, I think it was on the 7th of July, as they were digging this, Muhamed Merdan's son was severely wounded because he was also exchanged with him on the 17th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: In addition to trench-digging, were the prisoners used for other work or other operations in the field?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: From the statements of witnesses, from Rostokovici, who came to dig trenches in the area of Zubici, we only know that among other things, they were also used to dig out two bodies of killed. One was a member of the Armija, that is Samir, and they killed an HVO member there in that area. It was very difficult to dig him out, so these prisoners were also used to recover those bodies. We exchanged this Samir Perenda on the 13th of July, '93, and these prisoners also told them, when they came out of the camp, that they were also used to dig out -- for this kind of job. It happened one day only.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: I would like us to speak about another village now, the village of Isakovici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Lopez-Terres, I'm interrupting you for a moment. It seems to me that before we move to the next phase, that people had been used as human shields. I see that in the transcript. Could that be made more clear?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation)

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Could you give us some additional information about the use of prisoners when they had to go collect bodies on the battlefield?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I did not use the word "human shield." I did not say that. What I did say was that those captured Bosniaks who were taken from the camp in Senkovici the village of Zubici one day, and those were three prisoners, Semso Bradic and the other two names I do not know, but according to these witnesses, one day they were used between the lines of separation between the HVO army's and the BH army's units in the village of Zubici. They were used to recover the body of an Armija's member and one member of the HVO units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Lopez-Terres, we're coming to the time for the break. It may be convenient if you're moving on to another topic. Now, how much more do you have for this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) About 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll break now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. President, I believe that there's an interpretation error. We want to note this for the transcript. In French, the term "human shield" was used, which is not exactly the proper term.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. It wasn't, in fact, used in English, according to my recollection. Perhaps that could be sorted out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Witness C, I would like us now to speak about the attack on the village at Isakovici. During that attack which occurred in the beginning of October, 1993, did the BH army have any of its members taken prisoner by the HVO? How many soldiers were taken prisoner?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: On that day, five soldiers were taken prisoner in the area of the village of Isakovici, towards Streliste, at a place called Brgino Brdo. Five soldiers from the unit that was commanded by Saskic Atif.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: The attack on the village, was it carried out by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, yes. On that day, early in the morning, there was a strong attack by HVO units from the area of the village of Pribilovici, and all along this line which moved along the village of Isakovici towards the slopes of Mount Velenice, that is where the attack took place all day. Then also near the cemetery in the village of Isakovici there were about 30 dugouts, but then that line was recaptured in the afternoon and the army units already in the afternoon were at the positions where they were in the morning around 6.00 when the attack started. In addition to these soldiers who were captured, there were soldiers who were killed at this line too, and their bodies remained in between but the members of the army managed to get them out during the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: I would like you to talk to us more specifically about these five soldiers taken prisoner. Could you tell us what happened to three of them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: These five soldiers were Mutic Husein, Dedic Sevad, Hajric Enes, Mujak Nedzad, and Muslimovic Mevludin. On the 5th of October, that is to say, two days after this attack on the village of Isakovici, these captured soldiers who were brought to the region of Begino Brdo and they were tied up with mines. They had mines on their backs, and they came behind the line that was held by the BH army. We know for sure that in this human shield there were three soldiers, because one of them, Enes Hajric, went further up front, and he was almost to the BH army lines, and he was calling out to his son Hasan to shoot him, to kill him, because he did not want to remain a prisoner any longer. At that point in time, when he neared the line of the BH army, these mines were activated, because they were all connected by cable to the HVO soldiers, and all three of them were blown apart. The body of Enes Hajric was close to the army lines, and the members of the army managed to get him out on the 7th of October, 1993, and the bodies of the other two men who were killed were picked from the battlefield only on the 15th of November, 1993, when UNPROFOR mediated. Specifically, it was a Captain called York, whose headquarters were in Vitez, his unit was in Vitez. He was the one who mediated. The representatives of the army on that day, together with Captain York, came to the area of Begino Brdo and picked up the remains of the body of Mevludin Muslimovic, and Nedzad Mujak and the HVO side got the body of Borovickic Andjelko, its killed soldier. These three were used as a human shield because they wanted to retrieve the body of that soldier who was killed and that is why they tied them up and put these mines on their backs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: The HVO decided to send the three soldiers in order to pick up the body of an HVO soldier; is that correct? That's what they did?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. That is what we were told by Sevad Dedic, the surviving member of the BH army whom we exchanged a few days after that. Mutic Husein did not want to cross to the army side because he was married to a Croat woman, and he went to this part of Novi Travnik that was under HVO control. He did not want to be exchanged. So this is the information that I personally heard from this soldier, Dedic Sevad, the only survivor from amongst the five prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Remaining in October 1993, did the HVO soldiers shell the city of Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: On the 7th of October, there was a lot of shelling of the entire town during the day. The entire part of town that was under BH army was shelled and then this shelling stopped around 12.00 or 1.00 in the afternoon. Then sometime during the afternoon, between 4.00 and 5.00, three shells were launched against the town itself and, also, there was a mortar shell that was fired at the village of Kasapovici. This building, this is a civilian building that was called Mobilija, and this was the place where these shells had fallen. There were many civilians who were killed or wounded, and soldiers too, naturally, because this was in the afternoon hours. There was a market there too. This was between two buildings. They closed off an area, a U-shaped area. So this was an improvised market in the afternoon hours when there was less sniper fire, and that is where these two shells fell. Then two children were killed, and four children were wounded, and two civilians were killed too, middle-aged civilians, that is. Also, several soldiers who were in town at the time, that is to say, where the marketplace was. Among those who were killed on the 7th of October was also the son of Enes Hajric who was blown up by the mine on the 5th of October. On the 7th of October, his son, Hasan Hajric, was killed by this shell by the Mobilija building.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: The shelling that you're speaking about took place on the 7th of October. In October was there any further shelling on Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: There was another shelling. In the last week of October, I think it was the 23rd of October, but there weren't many civilians who were killed then as was the case on the 7th of October, there were only civilians who were wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: The two shelling incidents that you just spoke about were aimed against civilians; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, that's going to be a matter which we're going to have to decide. The witness can't say who they were aimed at.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation)

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Were there any military facilities in the areas that had come under shelling on that day in that area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. The closest building to the place that was hit was the building of the secondary school, and it was about 150 metres away from that building. That building was near the first army lines. Well, it depends really where you look at the line, but at the closest point perhaps it was 600 or 700 metres away from the line.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: In respect of the shelling of 7 October, you said that there were many casualties in the afternoon because they had been at a market at a moment when the sniper fire was not as heavy. Could you specify what you mean by that and to speak about those snipers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Sniper fire against the part of town that was under BH army control where civilians lived was there in October and, also, during all those nine months from June 1993 until February 1994. The sniper positions were in the area of the TV transmitter. I already mentioned that this was about a hundred metres away from the fire brigade building. From that place, the entire area that was under BH army control could be seen, that is, the street of the 4th of July and then the village of Isakovici. This part of town that was under BH army control, all of that was under sniper fire. Sometimes sniper fire was more intensive and sometimes it was not that intensive, but in this period, during sniper fire, that is to say, during these nine months there were many civilians who were killed and, naturally, soldiers as well during this nine-month period. Also, there were even more persons who were wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Could you give as you an estimate of the number of casualties on whom the snipers had been firing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: According to my very own data that I had collected, as I was staying in town at the time, and these are not complete data, this is only things I managed to learn since I was present when civilians were either killed or wounded, that part of town where the civilians lived were shelled and where there was sniper fire, according to my records there were 78 civilians who were either wounded or killed, and that includes the number of people who were killed on that previous day, the nine people who were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You produced a list of the victims, casualties. We're going to show you the list, and can you confirm that that is, in fact, the document that you gave us?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) The reference number is Z1962/2?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, this is the list that I compiled on the basis of my own notes from my war diary, the diary I kept. I did this for my own purposes. I made notes every day, ever since I became a member of the army in May 1992, until April 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation)

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Could you give us some information about the list? Could you specify who the people who were killed are and who were the ones who were wounded, in a few words, so that the Trial Chamber, which does not have a translation of the document, can identify who was killed? Who were the people who were killed and who were the ones who were wounded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Shall we start from the beginning?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Lopez-Terres, there ought to be a translation of this. The requirement is that documents, before they're exhibited, are translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I simply wanted to ask the witness to tell us what the meaning of the word in Serbo-Croat would be for killed or wounded so that the Trial Chamber could understand what corresponds to which victims whose names appear on the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can do that. Do it briefly, please, rather than going through the list, but in future, these documents should be translated before they're put into the Trial Chamber as exhibits. Can you just ask the witness what these words mean, not to go through the list, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation)

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Witness C, the word that I'm not going to pronounce very well, "poginuo", does that refer to a person who is dead?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. "Poginuo" is the word that is used for a person who was killed on the date that is mentioned on this list. I can mention a few examples, if you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: And the word "ranjen"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: These are civilian persons who were hit by sniper that day or wounded by shelling. It depends on the day concerned. "Ranjen" are persons who were not killed on the spot. Perhaps they passed away later, as they were being treated medically. Perhaps death came as a consequence of that wounding.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: To simplify things, the "poginuo" refers to a deceased person and the word "ranjen" refers to a wounded person; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Witness C, the Office of the Prosecutor has another document which has been shown to you, and that document was received from the Bosnia-Herzegovina authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) The document is Z1958. The document has a list of the BH army soldiers who died in combat both against the Serbian army and the HVO army. Could you review the document and paying special attention to the soldiers whose names are under numbers 58, 99. Could you confirm that those two names correspond to the names of the soldiers that you mentioned in your deposition?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. These are the soldiers that I mentioned in my previous statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Does that also apply to three other names? I ask you to look at number 119 -- as I said, 119, 121, and 171.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: One seventy one, that is the soldier I mentioned. His name was Cazo, nicknamed Cazo. Muhamed Sahinovic was his name. The probable date of death is mentioned here. However, there is a note here that says "massacred by HV." I think this is a mistake here. I think it should say "HVO." One hundred nineteen, as well, again this is the person that I mentioned, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Otherwise, I am aware of this list because according to this methodology, according to this layout, we sent reports to the command that was our superior, and that was within my sector, and it was the command of the armed forces that in August 1992 said that I, together with my colleague Kovacevic, was in charge of all affairs related to the funerals of killed BH army soldiers. So I was the member of the command who was in charge of this inter alia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: I would like to ask the witness one last question, and it has to do with expulsions, that is, of Bosnians from the surrounding villages and Novi Travnik itself. Witness C, could you tell us whether, during the period of the third conflict that you've spoken about, whether the expulsions of the citizens of Bosnian origin continued in the sectors under the HVO control?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: After the third conflict broke out on the 9th of June, there were practically no expulsions because there were hardly any Bosniaks left in that period, I mean, Bosniaks who would be living in the part of town that was under HVO control. The expulsions were practically completed on the 8th of June, 1993, when one last big group of inhabitants was expelled from that part of town. It was 69 families that were expelled on that day. I know that personally, because from December until the 1st of August, my wife worked in the municipal Secretariat for Housing Affairs, and she practically had to work on the housing problems of these persons who were expelled. The Bosniaks who remained after the 9th of June, 1993, in that part of town that was under HVO control, they were deported to the camp in Stojkovici after being picked up on the 13th of June. By the end of the conflict, there were only individual Bosniaks there who lived in mixed marriages with their spouses, who were either Serbs or Croats. This was a very small number. I know three or four such individuals who remained in that part of town throughout, that is to say, who were not expelled. For example, Halid Salajdzic and his brother, Salajdzic Hilmija.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You don't have to give the names of the people. In respect of the surrounding villages, the villages surrounding Novi Travnik, were any expulsions of populations of Bosnian origin carried out as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: The HVO units, from the 9th of June until the end of this conflict in February, 1994, practically entered only one area that was inhabited by Bosniaks. These are the inhabitants of the village of Lazine. In other parts, there was no movement of lines and the HVO units did not enter a single area where there was a Bosniak population, and therefore there could not have been any expulsions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you. I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Naumovski. Are you going to cross-examine?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Your Honours, very briefly, not to waste your time, I wish to remind Your Honours once again the problems facing the Defence because of the extraordinarily large number of translated statements of the witness which were given the Defence this April. However, in spite of all these difficulties, and mindful of time, because we also think that the factor of time is very important, so that the Defence counsel for Mr. Kordic have decided to proceed immediately to the cross-examination of Witness C.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Witness C, may I introduce myself? I'm Mitko Naumovski, and I'm one of the counsel for Mr. Dario Kordic. I will ask you a number of questions. Witness C, you're in the habit, evidently, of writing your personal diary?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, notes, diary. I always use these diaries, logbooks, agendas, and I have been writing throughout the war all that was happening, all the important things.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So you had the principal wartime diary between '92 until '96?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I was taking notes, my own personal notes, and in August, '92, I was charged by Mr. Refik Lendo to also take notes for the municipal headquarters. I continued to do so when the 308th Brigade was formed, so that I had the war log of the municipal headquarters and then the 308th Brigade throughout that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So to make it quite clear, you kept your personal diary, your own personal private notes, and as of the date that you said, you also began to keep the official diary or rather the official logbook of the BH army; is that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: In what capacity did you do it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: As a member of the municipal headquarters or, rather, as a member of the command of the 308th Brigade of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Tell us, please, you talked to the investigators of this Tribunal on several occasions, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Twice. And during your conversations with investigators, you used your diary?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: At times.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You used your personal diary, your private notes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
