utterances.text: Yes. I did not have any official logbook because it stayed behind in the archives of the brigade and I don't know where it ended up. I presume that it has all been turned over to the main archives of the chief of staff of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Yes. So we are talking about your private -- about your private diary, and it contains the same facts as the official logbook that you took; is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, it contains some of the facts that can be found in the official logbook. There were some which were of personal interest and which I then also entered in my private diary, but it is indubitably, in terms of scope and contents, much smaller, much narrower than the official one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But be that as it may, all the circumstances of relevance you also entered into your private diary, didn't you, your personal notes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: I wouldn't say all things of relevance. Some events were of relevance for a particular period and yet were not included in my private diary. But everything that was of import for the area of responsibility of this municipal headquarters and the brigade, according to the methodology as to what is to be entered into the war logbook, that was entered, of course, in this official logbook for which I was put in charge of and which I duly wrote every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Will you please focus on your private diary? We are talking about your private diary which you have, which is in your possession, which you have.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I also told you that in my personal diary, you will not find all the things of relevance that would have to be in the official one. They are not all included in my personal diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But you said that you used those notes during your interviews with investigators, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Now and then, I needed to look up a date or a name.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You had to prepare yourself to appear before The Hague Tribunal, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Not particularly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: My thoughts are in the direction of leafing through your notes, reading the notes that you have taken down for years.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I finished that when I made my statement, and that was, as far as I remember, in November, 1997, ending with the 3rd of December, '97. And after that, I did not refer particularly to these notes of mine. I simply tried, during that period of time, that is, subsequently, to forget, as much as I could, all that had come to pass to me during the war, all that befell me during the war, and I really had no wish to keep looking at the diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But my question referred only to preparations for the Tribunal, for this evidence, for this testimony. Did you read the notes from your diary before you came to the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, yes, I leafed through it casually.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Did you use those notes when you arrived here and since you arrived here, during your stay here?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not want to use them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But you have them with you, those notes of yours of your private diary?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: I have it with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You had it with you throughout your stay in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Will you be so kind as to tell the Court how long have you been in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: I arrived here on the 8th of April, in the afternoon hours sometime, around 4.00 or 5.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Do you have this diary with you today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Could the Court have the opportunity to check and compare your testimony today with your notes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, that's a matter to which, no doubt, we would have to decide, if you are applying to see the diary. But you would also have to have in mind the question of time. The witness has now been here 12 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: (Interpretation) If you're waiting for my answer, I shall reply immediately, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, that's why I raised it. Now, Mr. Naumovski, are you applying to see the diary?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: (Interpretation) All I wanted was to check whether the witness had that diary and whether he had an opportunity to read that diary since he has been here, that is, since the 8th of April, if I understood him properly, to this day. The Defence has not received that diary, so the Defence has had no opportunity of checking what was in the diary and juxtapose it to the testimony of this witness before this Court. Hence my question. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You've asked the witness, and he's answered in relation to that diary. Now, can we move on to something else?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Perhaps only a sentence from the diary, if I may. From your testimony here, it transpires that you wrote in your diary things that you eyewitnessed and also what you heard from some other sources; is that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. I noted down or recorded things that I thought important from my own point of view that happened that particular day, and it was also, in a way, in preparation for the official logbook that I had to keep. There was a prescribed methodology, and one knew exactly what kind of facts had to be recorded if anything happened, and so sometimes it was a source used when I kept the official logbook. So I do not call my diary a war diary. Those were simply my private notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Yes, I see. Let us cut this short and help the Court to save time. All I wanted to ask you, the last question about the diary, when you read the diary or when somebody else reads it, one cannot really distinguish which is your personal recollection of a particular event and things that you heard from somebody else and that were put down; is that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I can remember every fact that I put in because I know that diary. I almost know every page or part of the page which I wrote, so that it is -- it presents no problem for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Yes, but if a third person read it, that person would not be able to distinguish your personal knowledge from what you heard from others; is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, these are my personal notes, and for a third person, they would indubitably be a paper full of question marks, full of blank spaces, and they wouldn't be able to really understand it much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Right. Let us, then, move to another topic. But before we do so, a question related to your particulars. You graduated from university; we heard that. You did tell us so. However, you said nothing about the secondary education. So my question is did you complete the religious school, that is the Medresa?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. That was the secondary school I had come out from, and I immediately proceeded to university.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So you completed the Medresa in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And it lasted how long; five years?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: What title, what degree do you get, when you come out of that secondary school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: No particular degree, because it was a secondary school, but under the regulations that secondary school allowed one to also perform certain religious duties, that is, to become imams.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So this is the minimum education that an imam needs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: All right, thank you. Now I'm proceeding to a set of questions upon which I believe we shall agree upon because I don't think there will be any difficulties. The first question is the Croatian Defence Council and the Territorial Defence, subsequently, we said in the summer of '92, what came to be known as the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina were two components of one in the same armed forces, that is, the armed forces of the Republic of Boznia-Herzegovina; is that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: That was prescribed by the defence law and the armed forces law. I don't know the exact date when the text of the law on defence was changed. But it did, and there were some amendments to it which said that the HVO was also another element of the armed forces, together with the Ministry of the Interior forces and other armed formations, that is how it read, and the HVO was also a component of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That was the regulation adopted by the presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina submitted to the assembly and approved by the assembly of the Republic of Boznia-Herzegovina, and thus became a law.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Thank you. And my second question is we know that in July, '94, the Serbs of the former JNA and Serbs invaded your part of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and a question, therefore. Since the HVO and the TO formations were armed up to a degree, each one of them, each in its own sector, manned lines, I mean military lines, against the Serbs, did not they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: In '92 until '93, in the territory of the Novi Travnik municipality, there was indeed a defence line which went west of the municipality of Novi Travnik towards Donji Vakuf, where the BH army units and the HVO units manned the line against the Serb side, which then followed the same direction and roughly of the same length.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But we have to see that we are talking the same language, for the sake of interpretation. I have noted down here that the HVO held the lines at Kastel Grad, Karamlija, Kamenjas, Mravinjac, and the TO forces held the other line in the town of Turbe.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: That is not accurate. During one period of time, the HVO did, in 1992, reach Kastel Grad. However, afterwards the line was moved to the north and it ended somewhere in the region of Kamenjas above the village of Pecine. The Novi Travnik units of the army held the line to the left of the HVO units, and they went from the village of Grgici and then went to the plateau, and then to the south and south-west they went towards the units of Bugojno, that is to say, the units of the army in the region of Medina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Sorry, perhaps it would be better for the Honourable Judges if they saw you show this on the map. This is map 2.612, I think, point 3. 2.612,3. Please, Witness C, you don't have to do it in great detail. Just show the area that was held by the HVO and where the line was against the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Approximately here, this is where the HVO was. This is above the village of Djakovici and Mravinjac. Then I think this is 1293, and then it went to 510 where Kamenjas is. This is where the line ended. In May and June, 1993, this line did indeed go all the way to Ravno Rostovo and Kastel Grad. When the BH army units were from Ravno Rostovo, across the Zijamet, they advanced in that direction and they reached the village of Medina and another village below the village of Medina towards the village of Kopcici, rather, in the municipality of Bugojno. That's where the line went. So this is approximately where the line was on this right-hand side, that is, on the right flank. That is where the HVO unit was, so all the way down to the Bugojno units. This is where the BH army units from Novi Travnik were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Your Honours, with your permission, perhaps it would be a good thing if we would allow the witness to mark these lines that he spoke of on this map, with your permission. We can use a special colour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have we got another copy? It might be convenient not to use the original exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I'm willing to give our copy, and we are going to get another one later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Hand in your copy, please, Mr. Naumovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: (Interpretation)

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Please use this Magic Marker. I think it's purple. Watch out, the line will be pretty thick, so just mark it as carefully as you can, the line we talked about.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: It's a very small map, so it's a bit difficult, but this is the way it was, roughly. This is one line and this is the other line, the army units on the other side. But this line of defence that was held by the HVO finished on the 16th of June, 1993, when they withdrew towards the Serbian side, and then the units of the army in an eight-day period that followed, together with units from Travnik, were preparing an attack and took this line from the Serbs. It was handed over to the Serbs by the HVO soldiers, and it was held by the Serbs for eight days that --

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry. This is now this big conflict between the TO and the HVO in the summer, but I just wanted to have the undeniable facts there so we wouldn't have to discuss them any further, so thank you for showing us this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let that exhibit be marked 2612,3(a).

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: (Interpretation) That is exactly what I had wished to ask for.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Witness C, we can proceed. A few questions related to the first conflict. It was an incident, rather, and it occurred in June 1992. On that day, some 40 members of the Territorial Defence of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina were returning from the line they held against the Serbs; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, not on that day. On the previous day, the 18th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Oh, sorry. I was actually thinking of the 18th but I didn't say it. I'm actually thinking of the 18th. So we agree on that. When they were returning from their lines, they entered the town of Novi Travnik and they were moving through the villages of Nevic Polje, Bucici, Stojkovici; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Nevic Polje, Stojkovici, not Bucici. Bucici is outside that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Nevic Polje and Stojkovici are populated by Croats predominantly; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: These 40-odd soldiers that were returning to Novi Travnik, as they were passing in this direction that we mentioned, they used firearms to shoot. They were shooting in the air, I think, but they were using firearms; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know whether they were shooting in that direction. I personally know they were shooting as they were passing through town, and when they were passing in front of the building where the municipal headquarters of the Territorial Defence was, that is to say, through town itself where the seat of the municipal headquarters of the Territorial Defence was. I do not know whether they behaved the same way when they were passing along that part of the road which is five or six kilometres before the building that I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So you do not know anything about the shooting that took place in those villages, either personally or through the people who submitted information to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, not from them and not from my colleagues whom I spent that afternoon with or, rather, the 19th of June, in the afternoon, when we had these negotiations. Everybody was only talking about shooting through this part of town.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: This was in the street of Borisa Kidrica in Novi Travnik, and this was a short area between the municipal headquarters and all the way up to the elementary school as Defence counsel -- no. It is about a kilometre, 700 metres away from the bus station. That is where the line was or, rather, the roads where these soldiers were shooting in the air. This was an ugly practice, but it was rather customary when soldiers were coming back from defence lines. HVO soldiers and army soldiers did too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry, but I don't want you to go into that, just give me a "Yes" or "No" answer. The part of town that we are talking about where you say that you know these soldiers were shooting, that is the part of town where the command of the HVO was too?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: At that time, no. At that time they were in the building of the old hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: My point is that Novi Travnik is not a big town. The centre of town is not that big or, rather, it's quite small. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Novi Travnik is not a big city, and there are four parallel streets that go through Novi Travnik. Borisa Kidrica is to the right, and the street where the HVO headquarters was. The last one is on the left-hand side is the 4th Street. So this is a small town. So that was that locality or that is where the two respective headquarters were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: When I said "small town," I wished to say that a burst of gunfire from an automatic rifle resounds in this relatively small centre of town; doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, you can hear it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So you can hear it. Thank you. The Territorial Defence forces took certain areas during those days. As a member of the headquarters, the staff, you certainly know that. So my question and claim is as follows: The Territorial Defence forces took the elevation that is called Zubicki Gaj. This is an area that goes north of the village of Zubici; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. In those days there were no special captures of any positions or buildings in May 1992. After all, there was some kind of agreement between these commands, between these components as to who would be stationed where and how these facilities would be used, those that were available at that time in town, so that they could be used in order to station headquarters or whatever. Novi Travnik did not have a barracks or anything where the military could be put up. I'm talking about the town itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So you are telling the court, in relation to this incident that we're talking about and this conflict or incident, should I say, in June 1992, the Territorial Defence forces did not especially take this area of Zubicki Gaj?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Tell me, the Commander of the unit that was in Zubicki Gaj, Enes Grizic, was he the Commander?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know, because during that period of time that you're talking about --

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So you don't know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I don't know the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Tell me, please, the Territorial Defence defence forces took the hill of Osoj. The Commander was Meho Mehanovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: That area was not taken at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Do you know the name of this gentlemen, Meho Mehanovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Meho Mehanovic was later the Commander of a company. After the first battalion of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was set up in Novi Travnik, and it was set up on the 22nd of July, 1992. So that is to say, a month and more after the period that we are talking about now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But are you not trying to say that before this formally established battalion was there, the TO was not set up at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: There were certain units that were established according to regional staffs. These were platoons and very rarely were they companies.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So this was later only formally, from an organisational point of view, when the battalion was set up but, in effect, the units existed beforehand; didn't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. The regional staffs organised these units sometime late in May or, more precisely, at the beginning of June. That is when they were attached to -- these smaller platoons were attached to the staffs. Perhaps in bigger places there were companies. They were later brought together into the 1st or 2nd Battalion, et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Only for the record, are you talking about 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one more question regarding these events. Mr. Mevludin Berberovic, at the time, was the chief of staff at the time we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Not on the 19th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: When did he become the head?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: A little later. I can't be exact as to the date, but I think it must have been sometime in August -- July or August when he was assigned, because in June it was Salih Lobas who was the Commander in June. And what was Mr. Berberovic then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think he was a member of the headquarters. I think he was responsible for operative and instruction. He was a deputy commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So he was your colleague on the headquarters?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. He was a member of the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Thank you. I do not want really to waste too much time, so I should immediately like to pass on to the second conflict which, as you said, began on the 19th of October, '92. Although you mentioned during the evidence in chief about an event, about an incident which happened on the 18th of October, that is, a day before the conflict, you, nevertheless, said nothing about that. So I would have a couple of questions in this regard. That day an incident happened. I don't know whether we can call it a petrol station or a fuel depot, something in Novi Travnik. Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. That day in the afternoon --

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Excuse me, please. If I may, I shall do it slowly. You agree with what I just said? Did you say "Yes"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. There was a dispute about the fuel that was delivered to that petrol pump.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Do we agree that that petrol pump or the fuel depot was housed, that is, it was in the yard of the old hotel or, rather, right next to the old hotel where the HVO headquarters was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. That building was next to the old hotel, between the building -- I mean, a residential building and the old hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: That petrol station or the depot was used by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. The petrol station was ceded for use by a decree on the mobilisation of facilities to a private company. I think it was called the Petrolex owned by Mustafa Poljarevic. That was fuel which had arrived for that gentleman, and that the dispute arose whether his tank -- a tank would deliver petrol to this petrol station which had been given to him for use.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: When I said "use," I meant the immediate vicinity of that petrol station to the command of the HVO which was in that building. It is in that sense.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: That is quite true that is where the petrol station was, but it was given for use to Mr. Mustafa Poljarevic, that is, his private company.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: The incident broke out at that day, you say, only because the fuel was off-loaded there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: I mentioned that there were incidents on the 18th. The second incident, which also entailed casualties, happened in the evening hours near the bus station, which is about 115 metres away from the old hotel. On the bus-stop -- the bus-stop there was hit. We could not establish from which direction it came. A member of the BH army, Krnjic, if I may, and that was the second incident that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: I'm afraid we're moving too fast, and the Court really will not be clear about what we have said because we have not clarified the first incident. We did not say anything about the first one, that is, about the petrol station in the old hotel's yard?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I know nothing about that except that, the security that was round their building and in the old hotel itself did not allow this Mr. Poljarevic to off-load a tanker truck there at this petrol station which had been given to him for use months before. I simply no nothing about that. I presume that his tanker truck went back. I know nothing else. I know that that was one of the disputable -- one of the mood -- things that happened that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: I was about to tell you some details about this, but if you are saying that you don't remember, that is, that you know nothing else about it -- if you are telling the Court that you know nothing else about it, then we could move on.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: I really do not know anything else except that it was not allowed to leave the petrol at this petrol station.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So you are saying that you know nothing about whether HVO units came to that site in the yard of the HVO headquarters.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. I was not there at the time. I was in that building of the nursery next to the Partizanka building, because at noon the event took place. A charity event was taking place. It was a musical something, entertainment event. That day we tried to raise some money from the population in order to purchase equipment and armaments for the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Right. But we agreed that this was an incident which preceded the conflict on the 19th, and I assume that you recorded that incident in your diary.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. It was recorded as one of those sporadic moments but relevant to the conflict itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: No, but I mean you did write down something about it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: I must have.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Your Honours, when I mentioned the diary again and what the witness is saying now, I do understand that we do have the problem of time and the witness has been here much too long, but I'm afraid that I will have to suggest, and I am suggesting it now, to be allowed to have a look at what Witness C has of this diary or whatever he calls it, so the Defence, in view of the diary, could perhaps get ready for this cross-examination better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is the issue that we're concerned with here about the dispute about petrol? What is the relevance of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Your Honours, a conflict never breaks out by itself, it is always preceded by something. What happened on the 19th was preceded by what happened on the 18th. We're talking about a petrol station which was in the yard of a building in which the HVO headquarters were accommodated, that is, the building of the old hotel. I am not asking you to immediately decide on my suggestion. I simply wanted to ask you to bear in mind the situation that we are faced with. On the one hand, before this main hearing we received an extraordinarily large number of documents or, rather, late translations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't want to interrupt you, but we know that that is the position, and we have it in mind, but if we are to decide this matter, we want to know if you are applying, and I thought you were not, but are you now applying to see the diary? If you are applying, then we will consider the matter now. If you're not, perhaps we can move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: (Interpretation) We're applying, Your Honours, and that is what I was saying, because this was the first part of what I was going to say about these late translations, but the second one immediately follows. Witness C says he used this material when he gave his statements, his testimony, but the Defence has not been shown it. This is another reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Does the Prosecution want to say anything about this?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) The diary in question is not part of the exhibits that were attached to Witness C's deposition and, therefore, did not have to be disclosed to the Defence. The Office of the Prosecutor does not have a copy of that diary, has no document, has no -- takes no preferred position in respect of the Defence on that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But have you seen it, Mr. Lopez-Terres, yourself?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Are you asking me that question personally? Do you mean have I seen it myself?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I thought that you were speaking to the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor. I personally did not see the diary, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May I possibly just add a word or so? So far as I know, nobody on the Prosecution team has seen the diary and it would appear, therefore, it hasn't been relied upon for the purpose of giving testimony, save for the extent that the witness may have spoken of leafing through it, I think. The position is, as I understand it, but only very indirectly, the diary contains a lot of material, probably other than the material that's the subject matter of the testimony itself, and I would respectfully invite the court, before it goes any further by way of granting leave to the Defence to see the diary or any part of it, that it should ask the witness himself what his attitude is to its disclosure, because we simply don't know. Then, thereafter, at most the Court should consider revealing specific entries rather than allowing the Defence to go through the diary itself in detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, I'm not going to ask the witness his attitude to it because, ultimately, it's a matter for us, but what I am going to ask him is whether it contains private material or not because that is relevant to our consideration. Witness C, you've heard what I've mentioned. The application, as also you've heard, is that the Defence lawyers should have a copy of your diary or should have a look at the diary. It is something which we are now going to have to consider, but before we do so, since we don't know what is in it, I am going to ask you whether it contains private material of your own besides merely references to the events of the war. Can you help us on that, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: I have to point out once again that this is not a diary. These are my private notes. In the first sentence of my statement it says so, that I might be referring from time to time to my personal notes, at the request of the person who spoke to me to allow them to have a look at these notes or to allow a part of it to be copied, something that I have emphatically refused, to make a copy of even a selection of things from there because there are very many private notes, very personal notes, notes that mean something to me only and only me, and there are also parts which have nothing to do with the statement that I was making.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is what I wanted to ask you. Is there anything else about the notes you want to add, briefly, if you could, because we've got to consider the matter now.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: These are my personal notes and they are very private for me. I have never published them or given them to anyone to use as a public document. Even when I was asked by the chief of staff of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina when they asked for the personal documents to be handed over to the archives, that archives was made up last autumn, that is, autumn last year, I refused to hand it over. I simply said no, because I think these are my personal private notes and they have no significance for anyone but me. What was the official logbook, what was the wartime logbook, that is something else that I also made entries into and this is the property of the army of B and H. My notes, the notes that I kept, I wrote publicly and it was published on the first anniversary of the 308th Brigade. A booklet was published to commemorate it as a document which talks about how these armed forces came to be and how they evolved. So things that were for publication were published and I gave them for publication, but these are my private papers. This is not an official wartime logbook which already exists in the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. These are my personal private notes. I absolutely refuse anyone to look at it, to set their eyes on it but me, and I've already explained that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Naumovski, you can address this again briefly, please, because we want to rule on this matter. The point is made that these are the private notes of the witness. Now, do you still say that you ought to be allowed to see them, in those circumstances?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Your Honours, the Defence has no other possibilities. Witness C said that he indicated that -- in the beginning of his statement to say when he would be using parts from the diary, but we do not know -- it is not shown anywhere when he uses information from the diary and when he speaks of his own knowledge. We simply do not know the measure of it. Is what he's telling us about of his own knowledge or does it derive from his own diary that he prepared, and read, and is using in this cross-examination? The Defence must have the possibility of checking that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll consider this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The issue in this application is whether some personal notes made by the witness during the course of the war should be shown to the Defence. We have been told by the Prosecution and we accept that none of the team here in court have seen this document. It appears that the witness may have had it at the time that he made his original statement, but he did not give it to the investigator. He asserts and we accept that it contains private matter which he does not want revealed. If this document had been relied upon when the witness was giving his evidence, then indeed there may have been a case for it being disclosed to the Defence in order to test the witness's credibility. But that is not so. It was not relied upon by him. So for that reason, it should not be disclosed. But there is a further reason which we should take into consideration, and that is that this is by way of being a personal document, personal notes, and also containing private material, and the witness is entitled to assert his right to privacy in connection with those notes. Accordingly, we do not disclose them, we do not order they be disclosed. If a similar situation arises in relation to a future witness, then the practical course would be for the Defence to raise the matter well in advance with the Prosecution. The position then can be considered fully, and it may be that some reasonable compromise, balancing the rights to privacy and the rights to disclosure, can be arrived at, depending on the particular circumstances. But in this case, we're not going to allow the notes to be disclosed. Very well, we'll adjourn now to 2.35. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.05 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Naumovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you, Your Honours. First of all, I would like to ask for some assistance, please. In the meantime, we've established that the marks that Witness C made on the map are no good when the map is photocopied, you can't see them, so I wanted to ask the Trial Chamber if Mr. C could use a different pen to make the same marks as he did on the previous map so that everybody can see exactly what he marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you. Yes, there are the pens.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Please, Witness C, could you use this marker now to make the same marks? For example, blue can be the HVO units. Use a different colour, green perhaps, or any other colour, to mark the lines that were held by the BH army against the Serbs. Thank you very much. Could this please be the original of this document now, the one that we handed in? Mr. C, may we continue our conversation, please or, rather, our questioning?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: When we talked about the incidents in October or, rather -- well, yes, yes, in October, you said that there were a few, but we dwelled on the one that occurred on the 18th of October. Let us just repeat this and then go on. You said that you personally did not have any direct knowledge as to what happened then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, except as information that there were some problems with the fuel and this pump or, rather, we -- we actually went to this gasoline station owned by Mr. Puljarovic, and that is where we got fuel for BH army vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But you did not know that the TO units came in or whatever?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, no. I don't know anything about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Thank you. As you mentioned this conflict or, rather, this second conflict, the second incident in 1992, in October, you said that at headquarters you received information that there was a conflict in Vitez and in Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: At this point in time, I'm only interested in Vitez. You are saying to the Court that there were conflicts between the TO and the HVO in Vitez as well in October, 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, the commander at headquarters told us that he had information from the regional staff in Zenica that there were conflicts in this period in Vitez and in Gornji Vakuf. And as regards details and the actual proportions, I did not have any information. I don't know whether the commander knew more and didn't tell us more. That I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: That is information that you got through the command of the 3rd Corps, actually through your own command, so to speak; is that --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, no, the 3rd Corps wasn't there yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Well, all right. But then we're talking about the regional staff?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. This was, at any rate, higher up in the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Tell me, do you have any direct knowledge about a blockade in Ahmici or, rather, a roadblock in October of 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I have no personal information about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Do you have any notes, perhaps, from other sources in your diary in this connection?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: In connection with this, I never had the opportunity of hearing anything. This is the first I hear of it, from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: This was an intensive incident, and there was an exchange of gunfire between the members of the TO and the HVO?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, maybe you know about the details. I really don't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Oh, I see. You don't know anything about it. So I can conclude that the information you received from your superior command in Zenica, as you had put it, was not explained in any way, it was just this mere piece of information?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: That is what I was told or, rather, we were told by our commander. That is to say, they didn't go into any details concerning what happened in these two places. At the meeting of the staff, we were not presented any details in connection with events in other municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: I'm asking you about this because you testified about this in the examination-in-chief. Those were your words, that in Gornji Vakuf and Vitez, there were conflicts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: I just said that we received information from the superior command that there were conflicts in Gornji Vakuf and in Vitez, and I said what the source of this information was, as it was conveyed to us, the members of the staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Your former commander of the Territorial Defence staff, I think that is the same gentleman who appointed you to the post that you held, that was Mr. Mandzuka; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, for a short period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: He was also replaced sometime in May, 1992, and Refik Lendo came to be commander then; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't think he was replaced. I wouldn't put it that way. I was present at the staff meeting when this was discussed, and Mr. Saban Mandzuka asked to be relieved of this duty of head of municipal staff because we have now with us a man who is from Novi Travnik, and his family was there and his parents and brother, et cetera, and that he was a trained officer, and his assessment was that this other man would discharge defence duties more successfully in the municipality of Novi Travnik, so he asked for Refik Lendo to be appointed to this post instead of him. Whether an order followed from a higher command to this effect later on, that I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, Mr. Mandzuka voluntarily let a more capable man take his place, a more capable soldier, so to speak?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, Saban Mandzuka was a reserve officer, whereas the other person was an active officer in the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Since you already said that he was an officer in the former JNA, do you perhaps know where he came from when he arrived in Novi Travnik? I'm talking about Mr. Refik Lendo.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: As far as I know, and according to the information I had, he came somewhere from the area of Nes. He came to Novi Travnik on the 21st of May, 1992, and I talked to him the next day and the day after that. Then Refik Lendo told me that he came to Tuzla and to Vares, the first army checkpoint. This was the first few days. Then his other brother went to Vares, a policeman. He came to pick him up, and he brought him to Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Well, thank you for these details, but we really don't want to use up that much time. Thank you. But let us say, for the Honourable Trial Chamber, that Nes is a city in the Republic of Serbia, that is to say, nowadays, this is Yugoslavia, the Republic of Yugoslavia. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: (No audible response)

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Please, could you just say "Yes" because if you just nod your head, this doesn't enter into the transcript.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. C, I have a few questions about the military forces, so to speak. You were in the Territorial Defence staff for a longer period of time, and I'm sure that you have good information about this, so I wish to ask you the following: On the one hand, we are talking about the set up of the Territorial Defence. Could you tell us, please, about the first battalion that was established in July, 1992? How many men were in this battalion? Just give us a general number. You don't have to give us more specific information than that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: As far as I remember, and it was only in November that I managed to receive official information from the main staff, the battalion -- well, depending on what kind of battalion it was, whether it was infantry battalion --

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: I'm talking about the first battalion.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: The formation of a battalion meant 520 soldiers at a maximum, but I think that the battalion never had this many men. There was 20 or 30 per cent less men than was set in the original formation. The first battalion, when it was established, I remember this, it had about 380 soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: That is a number from July 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Now we can move on to the second battalion that was establish in August 1992. Again, could you please give us the number of soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I do not have specific information about the second battalion, but I think that they only had 60 to 70 per cent of the required manpower because mobilisation had not been carried out by the authorities in charge until then, because these were volunteers that were included in these regional units attached to regional staffs beforehand. So if this is 60 to 70 per cent, then perhaps this is a number that ranges between 350 and 400 soldiers. I don't have the exact figures.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: I did not understand what you said, what you said about these volunteers. Before that, there was war mobilisation that was declared. This was a state of war that was declared. This is August 1992.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But, please, for the sake of the interpreters, we have to wait a bit before we answer questions and put them. The interpreters have to do their job properly. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: It is correct that in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the presidency of Bosnia and Hezrzegovina they declared a state of war on the 20th of June 1992, that is when general mobilisation was also declared, but you can see the pace at which this took place, that is to say, bringing together the volunteers who volunteered in the Territorial Defence units late in April and primarily in the months of May and June 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Thank you. Now a question about the third battalion that was set up a month later, that is to say, in September 1992.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not say that the third battalion was established in September 1992. I said that its formation started sometime in September 1992 and it was completed sometime by mid-October 1992. I know that it is the third battalion that did not meet all the requirements to the greatest possible degree. They had met only a bit over 50 per cent of their requirements as established by the formation, that is to say, that they had a total of about 250 to 300 soldiers within that battalion. When it was officially established as a unit in October 1992, that is to say, when it got its commanders, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Let us complete the subject that we're discussing now and that is the establishment of the brigade. The brigade was establish, if I understood you correctly, at the end of 1992.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, yes. The 308th Brigade of the 3rd Corps of the BH army was established on the 17th of December, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: What was its manpower? How many soldiers did it have?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I was not in charge of personnel, so I really could not give you accurate information. I'm afraid that this would be improvisation which would be more harmful than useful.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Please, could you think about this? You have presented so many facts so far that you learned as an active officer in the Territorial Defence staff, because this was, after all, your regular job. You talked about so many things that were not your immediate duty.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: As regards these data, and registration, and what the manpower requirements were, that was in another department and that's why I don't want to go into all of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: All right. So you're trying to say that you don't know how to answer this question about the manpower in the brigade. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: I could not say precisely at that time how many soldiers the brigade numbered, so it was these three battalions with this percentage and, also, there were some other units that belonged to the formation of a brigade. So I really don't have any information about these other units.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: One of these units within the brigade was the military police; was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Tell us, please, when was the military police established in your area, that is to say, before the brigade was established in 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Military police, at the level of platoon, was established, I think, between the 10th and 15th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So we agree that this was before the first incident that occurred in Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. I already spoke about that. This unit was under attack, one of the points that was under attack, and I talked about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Thank you. During your testimony you often said that you received information from either the higher command or from your own commander about certain events among the HVO, that is to say, on the HVO side. I infer that you have some knowledge as to the forces of the HVO in 1992 and 1993.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: As a member of the staff, I did not have any specific information about the HVO forces and their strength in the territory of Novi Travnik and especially not in other areas. I only mentioned that I was aware of the fact that an HVO brigade was established in Novi Travnik at the beginning of November 1992, but I did not go into any estimations or did I present any figures, because I simply didn't have them. That is to say, what this brigade was composed of and how many soldiers were in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: In my question, I did not start from the end, that is to say, from the brigade of the HVO. I wanted you to tell the Honourable Court about the information that you had about the HVO from April 1992 until the brigade was established. Can you answer that question?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I don't have information about this, nor can I answer this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So you are telling the Court that as you were working in the staff of the Territorial Defence of Novi Travnik, you did not, you personally or others didn't tell you about this either, about the forces of the HVO at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I didn't have any information about this. Whether the commander had such information and to what extent, that I cannot assess.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Witness C, you say that for awhile, for a long while, you kept a wartime logbook, a journal, where you entered facts that you learned about. On the basis of what you are saying now, I am concluding that there is no mention about the HVO forces in the area in that logbook.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: There is a mention of them, but what I'm telling you is that this official logbook does not mention anywhere the number of units, their strength, or their structure, but forces, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Now, in what sense?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Meaning HVO units here and there, the name of the unit such as, for instance, the HVO Brigade in Novi Travnik name and the like.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So let us then conclude this topic. You are telling the Court that you cannot speak about HVO forces in April 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: I can about the forces which were about to be formed then. I already said that. When I arrived at the headquarters, I received colleagues who had already done that, the information that the staff of the HVO had been formed. They also mentioned who was the commander of the HVO staff. As for the composition, the units that had been formed by the time, their strength, I cannot say anything about that because those facts I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But perhaps you do have some knowledge at the time of the first incident in June 1992 about -- do you have some facts about the HVO strength?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. About the strength, I don't know even -- I do not know even the strength at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And the same question as to October 1992. Do you have any facts about the HVO strength?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, not about the strength, but the name of the units -- no, I don't have any knowledge about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And another question relating to this. Do you have any knowledge about the HVO forces in June 1993 in the area within your jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: I know that at the time there was Stjepan Tomasevic HVO Brigade, but how strong was it, what units it consisted of, this is, again, something that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So you do not even know about men, that is the strength, the number of men or anything?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness seems to indicate no with his head but he didn't say anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: (Interpretation)

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: When we're talking about forces, about military formations in the area of Novi Travnik, we also need to mention HOS, H-O-S. H-O-S is the acronym for Croatian liberation forces. I stand corrected. Defence forces. So Croat defence forces, HOS. Will you please tell the Court whose were these forces? Whose were these forces?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I suppose the name already says whose they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: I guess you understood my question, Witness C. The question is: Within what party did HOS operate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: As far as I know, HOS, the Croat defence force was formed by the Croat Party of Right. They first existed in Croatian, and I know that in May 1992, a HOS unit was also mentioned in Novi Travnik as having been formed yet. I've had an opportunity to hear, sometime on the 23rd of May when there was an incident with the Serb side in the area of Pavlovica, that that unit was some 50 soldiers strong and that it was commanded by some Suse Skopljakavic, I believe was his last name but I'm not sure about the first name.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So you did have some figures about the HOS, and you didn't have such figures on the HVO?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. These figures I heard at a meeting in the building where -- in the hotel building where the intelligence signal centre was because there, on the 23rd of May, I believe, the activities were being agreed upon related to a armed group of Serbs spotted in the area of Lugovi in Pavlovica. This meeting was attended by certain gentlemen who asked to hear the strength of units existing there which could be used there at the time, because at that time we were still talking about the joint operation against -- we were talking about the joint operation. It was then I heard this figure this Mr. Suse mentioned, when asked by Tolo, "How many commanders do you have?" He told him, "About 50 combatants."

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Explain to the Court what you and I understand very well. The Croat Party of Right is a separate autonomous political party; is it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes, it is a party in its own right in Croatia, and it is a party which was in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: In addition, I wanted to say this was a part which was quite independent of the HDZ. HDZ was one party of the Croat people, and the Croat Party of Right was another party.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I do know they have different names. Whether they were independent of each other, what was the relationship between them, I really don't know because I do not have any direct knowledge about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You say you know nothing about political programme of the Croat Party of Right in relation to Bosnia-Herzegovina and their idea?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, something as to their chief slogan, yes, I do, because once I was present when a gentleman of the Croat Party of Right was there too. I can't remember his name. That was summer of 1992. We were at Mr. Lendo's. I think it was July or August. Then I heard that gentleman say that the Armija and the HOS should, together, go to fight the Chetniks as far as the Drina. I was present only briefly there. The two of them continued there conversation but without the presence of any other members. I was only briefly -- I just heard that one slogan of his.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Witness C, we, coming from the region, know what it means, and far as the Drina, but the Court might not be aware of what it might mean. So you answered my question in part, but I'm afraid from what you said, the Court will not understand that particular slogan. So will you be so kind as to explain it better?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think it meant, if I understood the programme properly, if I understood their objective, then it was the struggle for Bosnia-Herzegovina, for the liberation of Bosnia and Herzegovina as a whole, because Bosnia-Herzegovina, as far as the Drina, it usually meant Bosnia-Herzegovina within its historical boundaries, that is, as far as the Drina River. The boundary between Serbia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is, if I understood that particular slogan properly, and this is my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Actually, we won't go into your opinions. I do not share that opinion of yours. But if it is your opinion, I do not think we should waste the Court's time with that, and I believe we can proceed. But before we move on, I should like to mention another thing with regard to the HOS. HOS, from what you said, was a separate party with a separate commander?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, in May.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Does that mean that as of May, '92, until the end of '92, in truth, in fact, in the territory of Novi Travnik, there were three military entities, the HVO, HOS and the TO, which then grew into the army of B and H?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I cannot be as specific as to until when this special HOS unit operated in the area of Novi Travnik, the municipality. According to some information, they stopped existing in that area as a special unit in August because in late August, when the oath of allegiance was taken by HVO members, according to information of people who attended that particular event, and it was public and happened in the territory of the town, there were no -- among those units, there was no HOS unit. When did they cease to exist and until when did they exist as a separate unit, I do not know. I could not give you even an approximate date.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But regardless of this lack of accuracy, I mean that you are not quite certain, but you agree with me that there were three separate military forces, regardless of their strength?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness has answered that question as best he can. No doubt it will be a matter for us to determine, in due course, whether there were three or not. Can we now move on?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: A question seems to spring into my mind while we're talking about the HOS. I suppose you remember the time before the Serbs conquered Jajce. Before Jajce fell, rather. Now, a few days before the fall of Jajce, a unit, led by Ante Prkacin, which was -- I suppose you know that -- was awarded the rank of general by President Izetbegovic, so he was leading a unit to Jajce to try to help the defenders of Jajce. Do you remember that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: I do not know about Prkacin, that he went with the unit at that time. I met Mr. Prkacin sometime in early November, once when he came to the building of the municipal headquarters because, reportedly at that time, he was already a member of the joint command which had been set up in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Commander Lendo told me that Ante Prkacin was a member of that joint command and that it was in that capacity that he came. It was sometime in early November when he visited the municipal defence headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: With this introduction, I merely wanted to remind you of that period of time, and my question will follow. Your units and your commander, Refik Lendo, would not allow these units to pass through when they went on Jajce; do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: I cannot agree, because I simply have no information about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You do not have any information about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: I have no information about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So it cannot be found in your wartime logbook?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But you are the only one who was charged with making entries in that journal?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So you have no knowledge about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: A while ago, a few sentences ago, you said something about the position of the Muslims in the town controlled by the HVO. Since you also kept your personal diary and also the logbook of the brigade, did you also gather information about the position of Croats in the territory controlled by the Muslim forces, that is, the Territorial Defence, that is, subsequently the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: I wasn't really out to gather that information. I merely indicated facts that I happened to learn.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: I shall try to be even more precise. Do you have any knowledge about what happened in Croat villages of Ruda, Pecine, Margetici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: I mentioned it in my statement. I do not see why I should repeat it. I even mentioned the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: I'm asking about the plight of the Croats.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: I have no information that there was any plight of the Croats in those villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: I'm referring to civilians, not the soldiers. So you're saying the Croats did not suffer anything, any plight, anything at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I don't know anything about that. There wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But don't you agree with me that this was the responsibility of your unit, of your brigade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. As of the 16th of June, '93, when that area was left by HVO units and also the population of those villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You will, I'm sure, be able to tell us about houses destroyed in those villages at the time when your brigade was responsible for that area.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: At the time when my brigade was in that area, and it was there in those villages for a very short period of time because it went to conquer the line which the HVO soldiers had handed over to Chetniks, between the 16th to 25th of June, when we took and recovered that line and advanced the line towards Chetniks, those villages remained very far behind the line where the BH army units were. I know that after that period of time from June until November, because I passed through those villages, and I know that in some villages there were devastated houses and demolished houses, with the exception of Gornja Pecine where Chetniks did enter during those seven days when we took the line at Kamenjas, and there we found a number of houses that had been set alight and demolished only in Gornje Pecine. In Hadzici, Zenetici, Pobrdani, Ruda, Donje Pecine, were villages behind the units of the BH army, and they were unscathed. But between June until the end of November, when we see that this line to the Jajce Brigade -- to the Jajce Brigade of the BH army, that was made of combatants from Jajce, then indeed in those villages there were devastated houses and demolished houses, but I do not know who did that. But behind the army units -- the houses behind the army units, these houses remained whole, in one piece, and those units who were not active in that area did not operate in that area, so we can't speak about demolished or devastated houses there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So we do agree, then, in these villages there was a number of destroyed houses, regardless of whether it was under your TO brigade or some other TO brigade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, passing through those parts on several occasions during that summer, I can say that, and that was my impression only, that the most houses were destroyed in the village of Kovacici, and those other villages, the destruction was not on a major scale, not even during that period of time. For a while at Ruda, there was a rear unit providing for the logistics and supply of the unit that was at Kamenjas, but I can affirm that in Ruda, not one house was destroyed by either civilians or soldiers while this logistics unit was there until November, 1993. I cannot say what the situation is at present because I have not been to that part for some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: What I asked you about pertains only to the period until the cease-fire was signed, that is to say, the 25th of February, 1994. That is to say, that the Defence has received the following information; that on the territory of the administrative municipality of Novi Travnik in this period up to that date that I mentioned, about 1.500 buildings owned by Croats were torched, demolished, devastated in some way. Do you know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. No, I have no specific information about this, except for this impression I had. That is to say that I saw these houses that were demolished in some villages, and any precise data as to how many houses and -- I imagine that other authorities do not have precise information to that effect either.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Now let us go back to the town of Novi Travnik with a few questions, although, Your Honours, I keep looking at the clock, too, but unfortunately I still have a few questions, so I beg for your indulgence. On these maps that the Prosecutor used in the examination-in-chief, you showed how the town was partitioned. You drew this line, and you could see who was where and who was in charge of what. However, I think that the geographical situation in Novi Travnik was not fully explained. So could you please tell us, this part that was under the Territorial Defence, later the BH army, isn't that higher up than the terrain held by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You are saying that it is not at a higher altitude than the northern part that was held by the HVO? You know this better than I do.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, geographically whether this is higher or lower as compared to the line of separation, that is unimportant. I'm talking about elevations around the town. That would probably be a factor to reckon with.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: I did not think in a military sense. I was not speaking of elevations in a military sense, I was simply talking about the terrain itself. Was it higher up or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I know that Kazapucni Poltuk flows from the south-west and it flows through that part.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: All right. So then my conclusion is correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, at least in terms of one metre, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us, please, this part of town where the Croats were that got water from this other part of town, that is to say, the waterworks went through the part of town that was held by the Territorial Defence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, that is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Was there waterworks, I mean, from Opara? I'm not good at this geography. You're better at it than I am.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, part of this waterworks went through Ravno Rostovo -- from Ravno Rostovo and, inter alia, went through Opara and Trenica, these villages, and that was the bigger water pipe that went that way, and then it goes through Hrastovci, that part of town or that part of the suburbs, and then it goes into town. This old water pipe, another one that was used in the old waterworks, that is in the region of that hill above Kasapovici and further up above Bratstvo, allegedly. It was in the water system, but I don't know exactly what the town waterworks is like.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: I put one question and you answer three questions. I asked whether the main waterworks went through the part of town that you held to the part of town that was held by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: It goes from part of the ground that was under army control, and then as it enters town from the suburbs onwards, perhaps a kilometre and a half or two kilometres, it goes through the zone that was behind HVO lines, and it goes into the town itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: I'm asking you this because we know that on the 27th of August, 1993, water was closed in that part of town that was held by the TO. Do you agree with that? Water was closed of course to that part of town that was held by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: If the water pipe was closed on the 27th of August, and if this was done in the region of Opara or towards the source, then it was closed for all the inhabitants that used that part of the waterworks. It was impossible to make that kind of selection, to keep it open for one part and closed for another part, because in the region of Pavlovici until it enters town, it is one waterworks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You haven't answered my question, Mr. C. Tell me, you are saying "if it was closed," and I asserted something. Do you agree with me that on the 27th of August, water was closed off for the part of town that was held by the HVO? That was the question, and, please, I would like a direct answer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know whether water was closed on that day and during those days, but I know for sure that there were many days in the months June, July and August, 1993, and even later, when the entire town was without water, even the building that I lived in, and it was about 50 metres away from the hotel building, that is to say, Bratstvo Novi Travnik, and we called it Partizanka.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. C, you are telling the Honourable Judges that you did not know that on the 27th of August, the water was not closed in your part of town, thus leaving the part of town held by HVO without any water?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Do you perhaps know of something else related to public utilities? We have also received information that in the summer of 1993, when there were water shortages in this part of town that was held by the HVO, sewage flew out of that part of town that was held by the HVO or into the part that was held by the HVO. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I don't know that, and I can't say anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You should know this because of the smell that must have come out of the part of town that was held by the HVO, because after all, this was the summer. I'm talking about the summer of '93. You must have smelled the smell.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: I didn't know that there were such problems in town, but I know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Naumovski, we will get on more quickly if, on receiving a reply, you don't argue the point with the witness. He said he didn't know about this outflow of sewage. That really ends the matter, and there's no point arguing with him about it. If I could address the witness for a moment. Could you please, Witness C, just answer the questions shortly? I hope we're going to be able to finish today.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
