utterances.text: (Interpretation) Yes, Your Honours, I absolutely accept the criticism addressed to me, and I shall try to refrain as much as possible. But this last question I put relates to the summer. This happened in the summer. It was so hot. And that is why I asked this additional question. I'm sorry. I won't do it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: The old high-rise, Stari Soliter as you call it, and it was marked as "1" in your map, was referred to many times today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: On the basis of what you said today, I infer that this old high-rise was the line of separation between the two sides. It was between the two sides; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, but it was 20 metres away from the Workers' Centre and about 30 to 40 metres from the line held by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: If I follow what you said very precisely, and I forgot whether you said it today or earlier on, that high-rise had been held by the HVO at some point, this number 1; had it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't really say that it was in their hands. It was used as a military facility in the October conflict in 1992, especially the 7th, 8th, 9th and 10th floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: By who?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: By HVO units. For three days, they were shooting against the high-rise where my family lived, and on this third day, on the 21st, it caught fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: At the time when the fighting was on, that is to say, when efforts were made to take this high-rise, and this is at the time when the people living in it were still there, high-rise number three was held by the Territorial Defence; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was the hands of the police, the police station, civilian police station in Novi Travnik. Its headquarters was right next door and they were in charge of that building.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Are you trying to tell the Court that high-rise number three, and that is the one that is marked on the map, it is practically across from high-rise one, in these actions we talked about it was not used as a military facility from the beginning, that is to say, from the 9th of June.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. When the conflict began in town, this building was inter alia a military facility, because it had burned down in October 1992 and it was empty. There was no one living there. There was no one there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: We are talking about the people who lived in high-rise number one, but high-rise number three was a military facility, a military stronghold; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You talked about this. You said that information was exchanged or, rather, that the possibility of releasing these people who were there was discussed; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: The first request came from the HVO, that they would allow the civilians to be evacuated on the condition that they were allowed to enter the building and use the old high-rise building as a military building, the one marked as one. The commission that negotiated about this at the beginning of July 1993, as authorised by the war presidency, they did not agree to this, and they did not let the HVO forces use this building on the 23rd, also on the condition of exchanging the civilians from that high-rise for the civilians from Senkovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: I understand what you're saying. The HVO was not opposed to the evacuation of civilians from these high-rises. They did not prevent this from taking place.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Their condition was that the HVO forces be allowed to enter the high-rise, and that the civilians leave, and that they continue to use that facility. According to the report of the commission and the president of this commission, that was submitted to the war presidency, and when the war presidency sought the opinion of the staff of the command of the brigade, the assessment was this was no guarantee for the civilians that they would be released if the HVO forces, the units of the HVO enter this high-rise as requested at the beginning of July 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: That is to say, that although the HVO forces did not prevent the civilians from leaving this building, you are saying that it was the conclusion of your commanders that this should not take place, and that is the reason why these civilians were not helped.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know if they wanted the civilians to leave the building. I am saying that they explicitly asked -- HVO explicitly asked, according to the information provided by the President of the commission for exchange, that the HVO forces wanted to enter this high-rise and that they were promising that they would release the civilians from that high-rise once they got into the building, but that was a condition that could not be met. It was the war presidency that made this decision. They only sought the opinion of the brigade. This was a commission that was set up by the war presidency of the municipality of Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: I think that the Honourable Judges understand what you've just said, so I don't want to repeat this, but I do have to repeat another thing. The HVO was not against the civilians leaving the building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: That is not a precise question. They wanted to get into the high-rise and to use it as a military facility, and then I'm saying, yes, the HVO wanted to enter the high-rise and use it as a military facility. Whether they were opposed to the civilians leaving the building or not, that I cannot go into.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: I would not have asked this had you not said that the HVO said that they would release the civilians. You said so today. That is why I'm insisting on this answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Naumovski, I think we have the point. Now, is there any dispute that the HVO said that the civilians could not leave unless the building was handed over to them? Is that in dispute, that that was the condition for the civilians leaving?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. President, the witness just said that their side had assessed that the Croats should not be trusted. He had said that a few minutes ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm not wanting to go back on what he said, but is there any dispute about that being the position?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: (Interpretation) The Croats wanted to release the civilians from the houses, if that's what you're asking me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So you're saying that the Croats wanted to release the civilians unconditionally.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: (Interpretation) At this point, it is difficult for me to be a witness in my own case, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm not asking you to be a witness, Mr. Naumovski. I'm asking you to do the thing which counsel should always be able to do, which is to tell the Court what their case is. Now, I'm asking you what your case is about. Is your case that the Croats were prepared to release the civilians without condition?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I just wanted to say that the Croats said that they would release these civilians if this high-rise is -- well, as the witness explained it, yes, because that is a follow-up to the story that came before this one, that is, October 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Naumovski, we want the position to be clear as to what your case is about, and we shall let you put one final question, putting to the witness what it is you say happened. One final question and then we move on. We shall sit, I may add, till 4.15, and if at all possible we shall finish this witness. Yes. Now, a final question on this business about the evacuation of the flats or flat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I will do that. If the Court believes this matter clarified, then I will not insist upon it any more. Our client, Mr. Kordic -- I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I do not regard it as clarified and I want it to be clarified. Do you agree with what the witness says, that the offer was to evacuate the flats, the high-rise, providing that the Croatian side took over the building? Now, do you accept that that was what was offered?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: (Interpretation) May I ask another question or do you want me to answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm asking you to answer the question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I agreed that there was an offer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: In those terms?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Let's move on then. As I say, if you can finish your cross-examination by 4.00, it will enable there to be any other examination and re-examination, and we can finish at 4.15. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you for the patience you're showing, Your Honours. I am sure that I will finish before 4.00, much before. Witness C, did the Serbs shell the town of Novi Travnik from time to time from the positions they were holding?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Serbs shelled Novi Travnik. The first time, I think, it was in June 1992, and that shelling was possible as long as the Serbs held the positions on Komar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Will you please be so kind and tell us how long were they able to shell it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Until the 13th of September, 1995, when the liberation of that area took place at Karaula, Komar, and, I think, Gornji Vakuf on that same date.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Right. So throughout that period of time, the Serbs could shell at both parts of the town of Novi Travnik. That is the one held by TO, that is BH army, and the one held by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. The whole area of the municipality, with the exception, perhaps, of the area of Pavlovica and Sebesic. All this was open to shelling from positions held by Serbs, that is, a wider region of combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Thank you. Will you tell us, please, you spoke about events in the town, and within the context you also mentioned snipers who operated from the area held by the HVO, if I understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, from the area of the TV transmitter, that is, the area of Osoje in the direction of the fire brigade centre, towards the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So far you were asked only about snipers from this side. Now I will ask you the following: The Defence learns that snipers also operated from the town which you held against the part of the town which was held by the HVO. Do you agree with this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So are you telling the Court that snipers never acted from the area of Novi Travnik held by the BH army or, rather, TO against the population in the part of the town kept by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: I do not know that there were any such snipers because at the staff of the brigade we never discussed about using the snipers in that part, but the BH army's line went through the town and I showed you where this line passed. So from this, one can say what was the range of rifles owned by the BH army soldiers all along that line that went through the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But this Croat part of the town, if I may call it so, the one held by the HVO, they had to go -- they had no water and they had to go to the suburbs. Some people fell victim to snipers in that part which was held by the HVO. That's why I'm asking you about that. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Is there anything in the brigade's logbook about this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, there isn't. About these phenomena we could not have any knowledge. There may have been civilian casualties on the other side but not something that we knew about, if there were any such casualties, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But tell us, did anybody have snipers apart from the regular, if I can call it that, army of the BH, those under your command? I'm referring to your territory.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, it is really difficult to be so precise when it comes to Bosnia-Herzegovina and who had what as of 1995, that is, May 1995, who had snipers or something else among the population and among others. One could find all sorts of things, because many people bought and paid for those things themselves, from pistols, guns, and so on and so forth. So I really don't know whether anyone had snipers' rifles or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But you have no knowledge whether, from your territory, that was under your control or somebody opened sniper power against the territory which was held by HVO?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. The soldiers of the BH army had orders, and there were a specific code of conduct which also prevented them from aiming at civilians and firing at civilians. They were also under such orders not to fire at them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But tell us, were there also some other units in the territory under your brigade that made part of the 3rd Corps or that came to make part of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Between June and February 1992 in our area, other units of the BH army also came from -- that is, those that made part of the 3rd Corps. I know specifically, and I already mentioned it, that there was a part of the 305th unit, those were the combatants of the Jajce -- army's combatants from Jajce, then 17th Krajina combatants also went through our territory. The units of the security service centre from Banja Luka, with their headquarters in Travnik, also went through our area and such like.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: In the territory of operation of your brigade, were there active or do you know whether the 7th Muslim Brigade or part thereof operated in that area within in the part of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: All I know is that sometime in July '93, when there was a smaller unit called Cobra, and I think it was part of the 17th Krajina Brigade, I think that together with them in our area, that is, in the area of Trenica and Zubici up to the TV transmitter, there was also a smaller unit. Some people say up to 50 soldiers, not more, from what subsequently became the 7th Muslim. Whether they were from that Muslim brigade from Travnik or from Zenica, I do not know, but I know that together with that unit, which belonged to the 17th Krajina, that unit was called Cobra, and in that area, that region, towards late July, that is, 1993, I also came across that information that a unit of the 7th Muslim was also there, but I wouldn't know whether they were also there during some other period of time or whether, during some other period of time, they were also units of the 7th Muslim present there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: I'm not sure if I heard the answer to my initial question that the units of the -- that the members of that unit were Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, in the colloquial used by HVO they were Mujahedin. I mean, that is how they termed them, but they were members of a unit which had the insignia of the BH army. Even the Bosniaks, sometimes in their vernacular, they were called Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But there was reason for that, don't you agree, why the Bosniaks called them Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any special reason for that, because in Arabic a fighter, a combatant, is a Mujahedid and Mujahedin is simply the plural of that noun. So it is an oriental term which has become part of the Bosniak language just as a number of other Turkish words and expressions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But you said Mujahedid, and that was a special unit within the 7th Muslim, as far as I know, but let's not tax the patience of the Court with this at the present. I wanted to ask you -- no, you wanted to say something.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: I believe I read in the press that it also comprised a detachment which was called El Mujahed, but I do not know that they ever came to the territory of the Novi Travnik municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You do know not who were those soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. I only read it in a magazine that reached me from the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: I think you said something. I think you used the word reportedly four soldiers of the HVO were abducted in 1993. Did I hear you well? Did you say "reportedly" or "allegedly"? That is what happened, four HVO officers were abducted on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Was it an abduction or not I really cannot say, but I know that in the talks as a reason for the tension or, rather, for the blockade, they mentioned the alleged abduction of those four soldiers, but what happened with those four or, I don't know how many of them, and how this whole episode ended, if they had indeed been captured, I really don't know, but I know this was mentioned as one of the chief reasons for the blockade which then took place on the 13th -- in the afternoon of April 13th.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: That blockade that you mentioned, it was something that was agreed between the commands of the HVO and the TO; wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: As far as I know, it was only agreed to jointly patrol -- to have mixed patrols of the HVO and BH army to patrol the Vodovod, Senkovici, down to Bugojno, because it was expected at that particular place an incident could have happened in that area, and I think that they agreed that they would go out to those sites jointly, I mean, members of the TO and the HVO, to visit this -- to patrol this whole area together where this incident might have happened that then gave rise to the blockade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But who was afraid that such an incident might be repeated? Was it a third party if the HVO and the TO were to control it together, to forestall any further incidents?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: I'll tell you right now. Those four HVO officers were, from what we know, were abducted by Mujahedin. That's what I asked you initially. After negotiations they were returned after a month, that is, in May 1993. Is there anything about that in your diary?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Except that I mention it as an incident and that it was assumed to have happened somewhere in the area of the Vodovod where the vehicle allegedly was left behind. The vehicle that they had been using before had been left. But what happened after that, about the investigation which was conducted by the military police or the army, I really do not know how this -- what was the final outcome of this whole, and what was the end result of this thing, and what happened to those four soldiers who had been allegedly abducted by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I do not remember that anyone explicitly mentioned that Mujahedin were responsible for it. There was a suspicion that they went missing in that area because the vehicle was found and there were no soldiers, and then at the headquarters it was agreed that we would know who participated in those talks, but in the evening hours when I came to the headquarters, it was agreed there should be a joint investigation related to the disappearance of those four soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: All right. So I won't press this point because you do not know the details. When we spoke about snipers a moment ago, I forget to mention one detail, that is, the Defence has also gathered some information about Croat civilian casualties in the municipality of Novi Travnik. Did you have an opportunity to read one of the books published in Novi Travnik and which contains the information about this, I mean, about the plight of the Croats there? In one of them, ten children are mentioned who were killed by -- some by sniper fire and some by shells. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: What I can say in my own name, and I want to assure both the Court and you that I am really very sorry for any civilian casualty that happened in Bosnia, and I really do not distinguish among the civilian casualties whatever their origin may be. I'm not prejudice. I'm not biased in any way, nor did I justify such things at any point in time. I do not know if there are such books. I read -- I usually read various weeklies. I did not read that, but as for Novi Travnik, yes, of course, I did read some other things about the civilian plight in other publications, in Dani, in Nova Bosna, Oslobodjenje, which I read, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: I asked you this because you've lived in Novi Travnik for many years and, therefore, you know all those people, those neighbours who lived there. Have you heard from others, from your neighbours, Croats, that there were casualties among children? Perhaps you learned about them from them? I don't really -- or the number of civilians who had been killed there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't. I do not really know any name, because I simply -- I communicated very little of late because of this situation there, and I practically only pass through a part of Novi Travnik and I do not really communicate much with people. So I do not know. I do not know the name of any civilian who perished there, not even the names of soldiers. I was very sorry when I learnt after the conflict that Mr. Milko Popovic, who participated in negotiations with me in 1992, that he had been killed during the war. I don't even know the circumstances or where or anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Right. Right. We won't go into that. I promised we would be finished by 4.00, at least I would be finished by 4.00. Just a moment ago and in only so many words, you mentioned the residents of the village of Senkovici and Torine. You said that those villagers did not want to leave the area which was held by the TO forces. Is that something that you know of your own knowledge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Directly in June 1992, when the conflict in Novi Travnik began and when the line of conflict was very far away from those villages, those residents stayed, of course, and those who wanted to, of course. There were some departures. Some Croats left those villages even before that, but a large number of them, and that was an exception in the municipality of Novi Travnik, that Croat residents remained living there after the conflict in the same area for another three months. Then in September, when there was a request for exchange, the majority of them said they wanted to leave because of the overall situation, that is, the food supplies and everything else that was happening in the area affected by the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: I know, of my own knowledge, I heard from a lady who was my neighbour, because in the spring of '93 I was planting and sewing my -- I was planting in the garden of (inaudible), and I remember we were doing something with the potatoes and green peas and --

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Let's cut it short.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: We were drinking water in front of a Croat's house, and they were living there, and they said that they would be staying there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But they expressed their free will to leave the area to an area held by Croats?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. In September, when I heard about this exchange for all, then the majority of them agreed to be exchanged and came to Novi Travnik and were exchanged. Well, they came on the 12th of July, and they exchanged with the HVO then. They procrastinated for another three or four days, so they had to spend several days in the secondary school, in an old block of buildings, and I think 120 or 130 of them spent several days there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Thank you. But you do not know for yourself whether they wanted to leave in August, for example, in '93?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I don't know that such requests were made by Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You don't know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, do you know -- I mean you should know, you kept a diary -- about the convoy that in October went to Osoje and Maglaj? Or, sorry, we're still at Pecine and Tuzla. I mean Pecine and Tuzla. Osoje is just a different name.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know what convoys are concerned. This is a route that was taken by convoys every day, practically.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: My question is: Do you know what happened to these convoys? Do you have any direct knowledge of this, and is there any mention of it in your diary?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: I know that in the war diary, it is only the Tuzla convoy that is mentioned or, rather, the incident related to it in Novi Travnik late in April.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But this is before that. This is Maglaj, Zepce, Tesanj and Tuzla, that convoy. Do you know anything about it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, no, I don't. This is in '92; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But, please, I'm asking you about something else now. The Mujahedin, at their checkpoint or roadblock that they held in Ravno Rostovo in January or February at that point, they stole a big parcel that was going to the operative command of Central Bosnia. Do you know anything about this theft?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, no, none whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Is there any trace of that in your personal diary?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Is there any trace of that in the diary of your brigade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: I really don't know. It's the first I hear of it. I first hear it from you now, so I don't know. You know all the details that occurred on the broader territory in this condition -- in these conditions of war --

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Well, Witness C, the Honourable Judges are here, and they are going to draw the relevant conclusions. We don't have to prove points to one another. Your Honours, just one more question on my part. How many times did you see Mr. Kordic from October, 1992, until the 25th of February, 1994?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (Resumed)
utterances.text: I already said that. We saw each other at the talks in Novi Travnik, and I don't remember ever seeing him, the mentioned gentleman, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you, Witness C. Thank you, Your Honours, for your patience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Your Honours, as Defence counsel for the other accused, and respectful of the fact that you said that we would be working until 4.15, and even with the best of intentions, I simply cannot complete my cross-examination by that time. Is it your decision that I should start the cross-examination now and continue tomorrow morning, or should I not start the cross-examination at all, or should I simply start cross-examination tomorrow and do it all in one stretch, which would be more convenient for the Defence? But I leave this in the hands of the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, how long are you going to be, do you think?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) My estimate is that I'll be needing between half an hour and one hour, 30 minutes to 60 minutes. Not more than that, at any rate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Tomorrow morning. Witness C, I'm afraid you must come back tomorrow, but we will conclude then. 9.45.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: 4.02 p.m., to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 21st day of April, 1999, at 9.45 a.m.
